All systems (4.6)–(4.30) admit the reduction U=𝟎U={\mathbf{0}}. From this viewpoint, (4.6)–(4.9), (4.10)–(4.12), (4.13)–(4.19) and (4.20)–(4.30) are generalizations of the 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order Burgers equation, the trivial equation ut=0u_{t}=0, the pKdV equation and the mKdV equation, respectively. Actually, (4.6)–(4.8) are the 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetries of the 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order systems (4.3)–(4.5), respectively.

4.2 Integrability of systems (4.3)–(4.30)

4.2.1 Systems (4.3) and (4.6)

We investigate the 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system (4.3) and its 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry (4.6) together. We note that the linear term ux​xu_{xx} in (4.3) vanishes iff a=−12a=-{1\over 2}, while the term ux​x​xu_{xxx} in (4.6) vanishes iff a=0a=0. This indicates that the case distinctions of a≠−12a\neq-{1\over 2} or a=−12a=-{1\over 2} and a≠0a\neq 0 or a=0a=0 are not very essential for the whole hierarchy of systems starting from (4.3). As an extension of the Hopf–Cole transformation, we consider the change of variables,

{w=e∫xu​d​x′,W=U​e12​∫xu​d​x′.\displaystyle\cases{w={\rm e}^{\int^{x}u\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptx^{\prime}}\vskip 4.2679pt\hskip-1.0pt,\cr W=U{\rm e}^{\frac{1}{2}\int^{x}u\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptx^{\prime}}\hskip-1.0pt.\cr}

Then we can triangular linearize (4.3) and (4.6) simultaneously as

{wt=13​(1+2​a)​wx​x+23​⟨W,W⟩,Wt=Wx​x,\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=\frac{1}{3}(1+2a)w_{xx}+\frac{2}{3}\langle W,W\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W_{t}=W_{xx},\cr} (4.31)

and

{wt=a​wx​x​x+⟨W,W⟩x,Wt=Wx​x​x.\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=aw_{xxx}+\langle W,W\rangle_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W_{t}=W_{xxx}.\cr} (4.32)

For some values of aa, we can solve these systems easily. When a=1a=1, we can fully linearize systems (4.31) and (4.32) through defining new variables VV and vv by W=VxW=V_{x}, w+13​⟨V,V⟩=vw+\frac{1}{3}\langle V,V\rangle=v (see [17]). When a=−12a=-{1\over 2}, we integrate the equation for ww in (4.31) to obtain

w⁡(x,t)=w⁡(x,0)+23​∫0t⟨W⁡(x,t′),W⁡(x,t′)⟩​d​t′.w(x,t)=w(x,0)+\frac{2}{3}\int^{t}_{0}\langle W(x,t^{\prime}),W(x,t^{\prime})\rangle\,{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptt^{\prime}.

Similarly, when a=0a=0, we can integrate the equation for ww in (4.32). We mention that Beukers, Sanders and Wang [37, 38] studied higher symmetries of the triangular linear systems (4.31) and (4.32) in the case of scalar WW.

Symmetrization. We discuss symmetrization for the 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system (4.3), since it is more fundamental than its 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry (4.6). To identify (4.3) as a multi-component generalization of a system in [18, 26], we assume the condition a≠−12a\neq-{1\over 2} and rescale variables as

∂t=13(1+2a)∂s,u=4u′,U=6U′.\partial_{t}=\frac{1}{3}(1+2a)\partial_{s},\hskip 14.22636ptu=4u^{\prime},\hskip 14.22636ptU=\sqrt{6}U^{\prime}.

In addition, we introduce a new parameter α\alpha by the relation

31+2​a=1−2​α,\frac{3}{1+2a}=1-2\alpha,

where α≠12\alpha\neq{1\over 2}. Then (4.3) is rewritten as

{us′=ux​x′+8​u′​ux′+(2−4​α)​⟨U′,Ux′⟩,Us′=(1−2​α)​Ux​x′−4​α​ux′​U′+(4−8​α)​u′​Ux′−(4+8​α)​u′ 2​U′−(2−4​α)​⟨U′,U′⟩​U′.\displaystyle\cases{u^{\prime}_{s}=u^{\prime}_{xx}+8u^{\prime}u^{\prime}_{x}+(2-4\alpha)\langle U^{\prime},U^{\prime}_{x}\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U^{\prime}_{s}=(1-2\alpha)U^{\prime}_{xx}-4\alpha u^{\prime}_{x}U^{\prime}+(4-8\alpha)u^{\prime}U^{\prime}_{x}-(4+8\alpha)u^{\prime\,2}U^{\prime}\cr\qquad\mbox{}-(2-4\alpha)\langle U^{\prime},U^{\prime}\rangle U^{\prime}.\cr}

In the case where U′U^{\prime} is scalar, this system is identical to (3.7) in [18]. In that case, considering the linear change of variables

u′=q+r,U′=q−r,u^{\prime}=q+r,\quad U^{\prime}=q-r,

we obtain a system of two symmetrically coupled Burgers equations, which coincides with (3.6) in [18] or (3.7) in [26]. We note that system (4.3) with a=−12a=-{1\over 2} does not have any counterpart in [18, 26], because of its degeneracy of the linear part (cf. the introduction).

4.2.2 Systems (4.4) and (4.7)

We investigate the 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system (4.4) and its 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry (4.7) together. Here, we note that (4.4) and (4.7) are obtained from (4.3) and (4.6), respectively, by rescaling tt, UU appropriately and taking the limit a→∞a\to\infty. Then, through the same change of variables as in section 4.2.1,

{w=e∫xu​d​x′,W=U​e12​∫xu​d​x′,\displaystyle\cases{w={\rm e}^{\int^{x}u\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptx^{\prime}}\vskip 4.2679pt\hskip-1.0pt,\cr W=U{\rm e}^{\frac{1}{2}\int^{x}u\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptx^{\prime}}\hskip-1.0pt,\cr}

we can transform systems (4.4) and (4.7) to

{wt=wx​x+⟨W,W⟩,Wt=𝟎,\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=w_{xx}+\langle W,W\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W_{t}=\mbox{\boldmath$0$},\cr} (4.33)

and

{wt=wx​x​x+⟨W,W⟩x,Wt=𝟎.\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=w_{xxx}+\langle W,W\rangle_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W_{t}=\mbox{\boldmath$0$}.\cr} (4.34)

Moreover, introducing a function g⁡(x)g(x) such that g′′​(x)=⟨W,W⟩g^{\prime\prime}(x)=\langle W,W\rangle, we can linearize the equations for ww in (4.33) and (4.34) with respect to the variable w+g⁡(x)w+g(x).

Symmetrization. We discuss symmetrization for the 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system (4.4). To identify (4.4) as a multi-component generalization of a system in [18, 26], we rescale the dependent variables as

u=4​u′,U=2​5​U′.u=4u^{\prime},\hskip 14.22636ptU=2\sqrt{5}U^{\prime}.

Then (4.4) is rewritten as

{ut′=ux​x′+8​u′​ux′+10​⟨U′,Ux′⟩,Ut′=−2​ux′​U′−8​u′ 2​U′−10​⟨U′,U′⟩​U′.\displaystyle\cases{u^{\prime}_{t}=u^{\prime}_{xx}+8u^{\prime}u^{\prime}_{x}+10\langle U^{\prime},U^{\prime}_{x}\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U^{\prime}_{t}=-2u^{\prime}_{x}U^{\prime}-8u^{\prime\,2}U^{\prime}-10\langle U^{\prime},U^{\prime}\rangle U^{\prime}.\cr}

In the case where U′U^{\prime} is scalar, this system should coincide with (3.10) in [18], if it were written correctly. Unfortunately, in [18], Foursov made a mistake in deriving the equation for zz in (3.10) from (3.9). It should be corrected as zt=−2​wx​z−8​w2​z−10​z3z_{t}=-2w_{x}z-8w^{2}z-10z^{3}. If we consider the linear change of variables

u′=q+r,U′=q−r,u^{\prime}=q+r,\quad U^{\prime}=q-r,

we obtain a system of two symmetrically coupled Burgers equations, which coincides with (3.9) in [18] or (3.6) in [26].

4.2.3 Systems (4.5) and (4.8)

We concentrate our attention on the 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system (4.5), and do not study its 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry (4.8). Defining a new variable ww by w≡12​⟨U,U⟩w\equiv\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle, we find that (4.5) contains a two-component Burgers system,

{ut=ux​x+2​u​ux+wx,wt=(u​w)x.\displaystyle\cases{u_{t}=u_{xx}+2uu_{x}+w_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr w_{t}=(uw)_{x}.\cr} (4.35)

Therefore, system (4.5) is a triangular system that consists of the Burgers system (4.35) and the linear equation for UU with Burgers-system-dependent coefficients. We mention that in the long-wave limit (disappearance of ux​xu_{xx}), (4.35) reduces to the Leroux system and that (4.35) can be rewritten as a non-evolutionary scalar equation in (at least) two different ways. The symmetry integrability of (4.35) as well as the existence of a recursion operator has already been demonstrated [18, 62]. Nevertheless, we could find neither a linearizing transformation nor a true Lax representation for (4.35). In what follows, we discuss travelling-wave solutions of (4.35), which are expected to give useful information on its properties.

Substituting the travelling-wave form

u⁡(x,t)=f⁡(z)−a,w⁡(x,t)=g⁡(z),z=x−a​t,u(x,t)=f(z)-a,\hskip 14.22636ptw(x,t)=g(z),\hskip 14.22636ptz=x-at,

into (4.35), we get a system of two ordinary differential equations. Integrating it once, we obtain

{f′+f2−a​f+g+b=0,f​g+c=0.\displaystyle\cases{f^{\prime}+f^{2}-af+g+b=0\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr fg+c=0.\cr} (4.36)

Here, bb and cc are integration constants that are determined from the boundary conditions for uu and ww. Plunging g=−c/fg=-c/f into the first equation in (4.36), we obtain the ordinary differential equation for ff,

d​fd​z=−f3−a​f2+b​f−cf.\frac{{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptf}{{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptz}=-\frac{f^{3}-af^{2}+bf-c}{f}. (4.37)

For the sake of simplicity, we assume that f3−a​f2+b​f−cf^{3}-af^{2}+bf-c can be factorized into the product (f−α1)​(f−α2)​(f−α3)(f-\alpha_{1})(f-\alpha_{2})(f-\alpha_{3}) with three distinct real roots α1,α2,α3\alpha_{1},\alpha_{2},\alpha_{3}. Thus we have

a=α1+α2+α3,b=α1​α2+α2​α3+α3​α1,c=α1​α2​α3.a=\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{3},\hskip 14.22636ptb=\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}+\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}+\alpha_{3}\alpha_{1},\hskip 14.22636ptc=\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}\alpha_{3}.

Furthermore, we assume the conditions αj≠0​(j=1,2,3)\alpha_{j}\neq 0\;(j=1,2,3) to obtain nontrivial solutions of (4.35). Indeed, if αj=0\alpha_{j}=0, then c=0c=0 and we obtain from (4.36) either a trivial solution or a solution of the scalar Burgers equation. Noting the identity

f(f−α1)​(f−α2)​(f−α3)\displaystyle\frac{f}{(f-\alpha_{1})(f-\alpha_{2})(f-\alpha_{3})} =\displaystyle\hskip-4.2679pt=\hskip-4.2679pt α1(α1−α2)​(α1−α3)​(1f−α1−1f−α3)\displaystyle\frac{\alpha_{1}}{(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{3})}\left(\frac{1}{f-\alpha_{1}}-\frac{1}{f-\alpha_{3}}\right)
+α2(α2−α1)​(α2−α3)​(1f−α2−1f−α3),\displaystyle\mbox{}+\frac{\alpha_{2}}{(\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1})(\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{3})}\left(\frac{1}{f-\alpha_{2}}-\frac{1}{f-\alpha_{3}}\right),

we can integrate (4.37) to obtain

(1+α3−α1f−α3)α1(α1−α2)​(α1−α3)​(1+α3−α2f−α3)α2(α2−α1)​(α2−α3)=d​e−z,\displaystyle\left(1+\frac{\alpha_{3}-\alpha_{1}}{f-\alpha_{3}}\right)^{\frac{\alpha_{1}}{(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{3})}}\left(1+\frac{\alpha_{3}-\alpha_{2}}{f-\alpha_{3}}\right)^{\frac{\alpha_{2}}{(\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{1})(\alpha_{2}-\alpha_{3})}}=d{\rm e}^{-z}, (4.38)

where dd is a constant. Now, it is clear that the functional form of 1/(f−α3)1/(f-\alpha_{3}) depends on the ratio of two powers on the left-hand side, (α3−1−α2−1)/(α1−1−α3−1)(\alpha_{3}^{-1}-\alpha_{2}^{-1})/(\alpha_{1}^{-1}-\alpha_{3}^{-1}). Let us consider the simplest case in which this ratio is unity, i.e.,

1α3=12​(1α1+1α2).\frac{1}{\alpha_{3}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha_{1}}+\frac{1}{\alpha_{2}}\right).

In this case, we have α1+α2≠0\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}\neq 0 for the existence of α3\alpha_{3}. Then we can solve (4.38) explicitly for 1/(f−α3)1/(f-\alpha_{3}):

1f−α3=−α1+α2+(α1+α2)2α1−α2​1+exp⁡[−(α1−α2)2α1+α2​(z−z0)]2​α1​α2.\displaystyle\frac{1}{f-\alpha_{3}}=-\frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\frac{(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})^{2}}{\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}}\sqrt{1+\exp\left[-\frac{(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})^{2}}{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}(z-z_{0})\right]}}{2\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}. (4.39)

Here, z0z_{0} is the constant given by

ez0≡d​[−4​α1​α2(α1+α2)2]α1+α2(α1−α2)2.{\rm e}^{z_{0}}\equiv d\left[\frac{-4\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}{(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})^{2}}\right]^{\frac{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}{(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})^{2}}}.

Using the relation α3=2​α1​α2/(α1+α2)\alpha_{3}=2\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}/(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}), we can rewrite (4.39) as

f⁡(z)=2​α1​α2α1+α2+α1−α21+exp⁡[−(α1−α2)2α1+α2​(z−z0)].f(z)=\frac{2\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}}{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+\frac{\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2}}{\sqrt{1+\exp\left[-\frac{(\alpha_{1}-\alpha_{2})^{2}}{\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}}(z-z_{0})\right]}}}. (4.40)

In order for the function f⁡(z)f(z) to be non-singular, we should assume the condition α1​(α1+α2)>0\alpha_{1}(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2})>0. To summarize, we have obtained in the simplest case a travelling-wave solution of (4.35) given by

u⁡(x,t)=f⁡(x−a​t)−a,w⁡(x,t)=−cf⁡(x−a​t),u(x,t)=f(x-at)-a,\hskip 14.22636ptw(x,t)=-\frac{c}{f(x-at)},

with (4.40), a=α1+α2+2​α1​α2/(α1+α2)a=\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}+2\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2}/(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}) and c=2​(α1​α2)2/(α1+α2)c=2(\alpha_{1}\alpha_{2})^{2}/(\alpha_{1}+\alpha_{2}).

When a nontrivial solution, like the above, of subsystem (4.35) is given, we can solve the remaining equation for UU in the original system (4.5), (Uj2)t=(u​Uj2)x\bigl(U_{j}^{2}\bigr)_{t}=\bigl(uU_{j}^{2}\bigr)_{x}, in the same way as in section 3.2.3.

Symmetrization. We discuss symmetrization for the 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system (4.5). With the rescaling of dependent variables

u=2​u′,U=6​U′,u=2u^{\prime},\hskip 14.22636ptU=\sqrt{6}U^{\prime},

(4.5) is rewritten as

{ut′=ux​x′+4​u′​ux′+3​⟨U′,Ux′⟩,Ut′=ux′​U′+2​u′​Ux′.\displaystyle\cases{u^{\prime}_{t}=u^{\prime}_{xx}+4u^{\prime}u^{\prime}_{x}+3\langle U^{\prime},U^{\prime}_{x}\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U^{\prime}_{t}=u^{\prime}_{x}U^{\prime}+2u^{\prime}U^{\prime}_{x}.\cr}

In the case where U′U^{\prime} is scalar, this system is identical to (3.4) in [18]. If we consider the linear change of variables

u′=q+r,U′=q−r,u^{\prime}=q+r,\quad U^{\prime}=q-r,

we obtain a system of two symmetrically coupled Burgers equations, which coincides with (3.3) in [18] or (3.5) in [26].

4.2.4 System (4.9)

In the case where UU is scalar, system (4.9) coincides with system (4.8). However, unlike (4.8), (4.9) in the general NN case does not possess a 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order symmetry of the form (4.1). System (4.9) contains the 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry of the two-component Burgers system (4.35), where ww is again given by w=12​⟨U,U⟩w=\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle. Therefore, in order to demonstrate the integrability of (4.9), we first of all need to know either a linearizing transformation or a Lax representation for (4.35). This remains as an open question.

Symmetrization. Through symmetrization of (4.9) in the case of scalar UU, we just obtain the 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry of the two symmetrically coupled Burgers equations in section 4.2.3.

4.2.5 System (4.10)

System (4.10) is connected with system (4.12) through a Miura-type transformation. We discuss the integrability of these two systems in section 4.2.7.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=α​(q−r).u=q+r,\quad U=\sqrt{\alpha}(q-r).

Here, α\alpha is a nonzero constant. Then we can rewrite (4.10) as a system of two symmetrically coupled equations,

{qt=12​qx​x​x−12​rx​x​x+12​(1+3​α)​(q−r)​qx​x+12​(1−3​α)​(q−r)​rx​x+12​qx2−12​rx2+3​α​(q−r)2​rx−32​α2​(q−r)4,rt=−12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x−12​(1−3​α)​(q−r)​qx​x−12​(1+3​α)​(q−r)​rx​x−12​qx2+12​rx2+3​α​(q−r)2​qx−32​α2​(q−r)4.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}-\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}(1+3\alpha)(q-r)q_{xx}+\frac{1}{2}(1-3\alpha)(q-r)r_{xx}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+\frac{1}{2}q_{x}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}r_{x}^{2}+3\alpha(q-r)^{2}r_{x}-\frac{3}{2}\alpha^{2}(q-r)^{4}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}-\frac{1}{2}(1-3\alpha)(q-r)q_{xx}-\frac{1}{2}(1+3\alpha)(q-r)r_{xx}\cr\qquad\mbox{}-\frac{1}{2}q_{x}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}r_{x}^{2}+3\alpha(q-r)^{2}q_{x}-\frac{3}{2}\alpha^{2}(q-r)^{4}.\cr}

This system does not belong to the class of systems studied in [25, 26], because of its degeneracy of the linear part.

4.2.6 System (4.11)

For system (4.11), we have the relation (ux−⟨U,U⟩)t=0(u_{x}-\langle U,U\rangle)_{t}=0. Thus, we can set

ux−⟨U,U⟩≡ϕ⁡(x),u_{x}-\langle U,U\rangle\equiv\phi(x), (4.41)

where the function ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) does not depend on tt. Then the equation for UU is rewritten in terms of ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) as

Ut=Ux​x​x+2​ϕ​Ux+ϕx​U.U_{t}=U_{xxx}+2\phi U_{x}+\phi_{x}U. (4.42)

The solutions of (4.42) are given by

U⁡(x,t)=∫d​λ​eλ​t​Ψ​(x,λ),U(x,t)=\int{\rm d}\hskip 0.0pt\lambda\,{\rm e}^{\lambda t}\Psi(x;\lambda),

where Ψ⁡(x,λ)\Psi(x;\lambda) is a solution of the ordinary differential equation

Ψx​x​x+2​ϕ​Ψx+ϕx​Ψ=λ​Ψ.\Psi_{xxx}+2\phi\Psi_{x}+\phi_{x}\Psi=\lambda\Psi. (4.43)

Once we obtain ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) and U⁡(x,t)U(x,t), we can determine u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) by using (4.41). The vector equation (4.43) is of the same form as the scattering problem associated with the Kaup–Kupershmidt equation [63, 64]. We can see that this is not a coincidence through investigation of the 5th 5^{\mbox{\scriptsize th }}order symmetry of system (4.11). Indeed, the 5th 5^{\mbox{\scriptsize th }}order symmetry is rewritten (up to a scaling of t5t_{5}) in terms of ϕ\phi and Ψ\Psi as

{ϕt5+ϕx​x​x​x​x+10​ϕ​ϕx​x​x+25​ϕx​ϕx​x+20​ϕ2​ϕx=0,Ψt5=9​Ψx​x​x​x​x+30​ϕ​Ψx​x​x+45​ϕx​Ψx​x+(35​ϕx​x+20​ϕ2)​Ψx+(10​ϕx​x​x+20​ϕ​ϕx)​Ψ.\displaystyle\cases{\phi_{t_{5}}+\phi_{xxxxx}+10\phi\phi_{xxx}+25\phi_{x}\phi_{xx}+20\phi^{2}\phi_{x}=0\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr\Psi_{t_{5}}=9\Psi_{xxxxx}+30\phi\Psi_{xxx}+45\phi_{x}\Psi_{xx}+(35\phi_{xx}+20\phi^{2})\Psi_{x}\cr\qquad\;\hskip 1.0pt\mbox{}+(10\phi_{xxx}+20\phi\phi_{x})\Psi.\cr}

The first equation is nothing but the Kaup–Kupershmidt equation, while the second equation together with (4.43) constitutes a Lax representation for it.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=α​(q−r).u=q+r,\quad U=\sqrt{\alpha}(q-r).

Here, α\alpha is a nonzero constant. Then we can rewrite (4.11) as a system of two symmetrically coupled equations,

{qt=12​qx​x​x−12​rx​x​x+(12+α)​(q−r)​qx​x+(12−α)​(q−r)​rx​x+(1−12​α)​qx2+α​qx​rx−(1+12​α)​rx2−α​(q−r)2​qx+3​α​(q−r)2​rx−α2​(q−r)4,rt=−12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x−(12−α)​(q−r)​qx​x−(12+α)​(q−r)​rx​x−(1+12​α)​qx2+α​qx​rx+(1−12​α)​rx2+3​α​(q−r)2​qx−α​(q−r)2​rx−α2​(q−r)4.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}-\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+(\frac{1}{2}+\alpha)(q-r)q_{xx}+(\frac{1}{2}-\alpha)(q-r)r_{xx}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+(1-\frac{1}{2}\alpha)q_{x}^{2}+\alpha q_{x}r_{x}-(1+\frac{1}{2}\alpha)r_{x}^{2}-\alpha(q-r)^{2}q_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+3\alpha(q-r)^{2}r_{x}-\alpha^{2}(q-r)^{4}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}-(\frac{1}{2}-\alpha)(q-r)q_{xx}-(\frac{1}{2}+\alpha)(q-r)r_{xx}\cr\qquad\mbox{}-(1+\frac{1}{2}\alpha)q_{x}^{2}+\alpha q_{x}r_{x}+(1-\frac{1}{2}\alpha)r_{x}^{2}+3\alpha(q-r)^{2}q_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}-\alpha(q-r)^{2}r_{x}-\alpha^{2}(q-r)^{4}.\cr}

This system does not belong to the class of nondegenerate systems studied in [25, 26].

4.2.7 System (4.12)

For system (4.12), if we define new variables ww and WW by

{w≡−ux−12​u2+12​⟨U,U⟩,W≡Ux+u​U,\displaystyle\cases{w\equiv-u_{x}-\frac{1}{2}u^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W\equiv U_{x}+uU,\cr} (4.44)

they satisfy the following system:

{wt=−3​⟨W,Wx⟩,Wt=Wx​x​x+wx​W+2​w​Wx.\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=-3\langle W,W_{x}\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W_{t}=W_{xxx}+w_{x}W+2wW_{x}.\cr} (4.45)

This system coincides with the multi-component Drinfel’d–Sokolov system (3.3), up to a scaling of WW. The Miura map (4.44) is a multi-component generalization of that for the case of scalar UU in [43, 44].

Relation to system (4.10)(\ref{sol1}). If we introduce a new scalar variable vv by

v≡ux−u2+⟨U,U⟩,v\equiv u_{x}-u^{2}+\langle U,U\rangle, (4.46)

system (4.12) is changed into the following system:

{vt=(3​v​⟨U,U⟩+3​⟨U,Ux​x⟩−3​⟨U,U⟩2)x,Ut=Ux​x​x+vx​U+v​Ux−3​⟨U,Ux⟩​U.\displaystyle\cases{v_{t}=\bigl(3v\langle U,U\rangle+3\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle-3\langle U,U\rangle^{2}\bigr)_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=U_{xxx}+v_{x}U+vU_{x}-3\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U.\cr} (4.47)

Then, it is straightforward to obtain (4.10) (for u^\hat{u} and UU) from (4.47) through potentiation v=u^xv=\hat{u}_{x}. Combining (4.46) and (4.44), we obtain the relation v−2​w=3​uxv-2w=3u_{x}, and consequently,

u^−2​∫xw​d​x′=3​u.\hat{u}-2\int^{x}w\,{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptx^{\prime}=3u.

Using this relation, we can also rewrite (4.44) as a transformation between system (4.10) and the multi-component Drinfel’d–Sokolov system (4.45).

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=α​(q−r).u=q+r,\quad U=\sqrt{\alpha}(q-r).

Here, α\alpha is a nonzero constant. Then we can rewrite (4.12) as a system of two symmetrically coupled equations,

{qt=12[qx​x−rx​x+(1+α)(q−r)qx+(1−α)(q−r)rx−(1−α)q3−(1+α)q2r+(1−α)qr2+(1+α)r3]x,rt=12[−qx​x+rx​x−(1−α)(q−r)qx−(1+α)(q−r)rx+(1+α)q3+(1−α)q2r−(1+α)qr2−(1−α)r3]x.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\bigl[q_{xx}-r_{xx}+(1+\alpha)(q-r)q_{x}+(1-\alpha)(q-r)r_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}-(1-\alpha)q^{3}-(1+\alpha)q^{2}r+(1-\alpha)qr^{2}+(1+\alpha)r^{3}\bigr]_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\frac{1}{2}\bigl[-q_{xx}+r_{xx}-(1-\alpha)(q-r)q_{x}-(1+\alpha)(q-r)r_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+(1+\alpha)q^{3}+(1-\alpha)q^{2}r-(1+\alpha)qr^{2}-(1-\alpha)r^{3}\bigr]_{x}.\cr} (4.48)

This system does not belong to the class of nondegenerate systems studied in [25, 26]. However, it was found in connection with the Kac–Moody Lie algebras and written in a Hamiltonian form about twenty years ago [43, 44]. More specifically, system (4.48) with α=−1\alpha=-1 coincides with (3)–(4) in [43] for the D3(2){\rm D}_{3}^{(2)} case, up to a scaling of variables (see also the generalized mKdV equation in [44] for the A3(2){\rm A}_{3}^{(2)} case).

4.2.8 System (4.13)

System (4.13) is merely a potential form of the multi-component Zakharov–Ito system (3.5).

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we set

u=q+r,U=q−r.u=q+r,\quad U=q-r.

Then we can rewrite (4.13) as a system of two symmetrically coupled pKdV equations,

{qt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+2​qx2+rx2,rt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+qx2+2​rx2.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+2q_{x}^{2}+r_{x}^{2}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+q_{x}^{2}+2r_{x}^{2}.\cr}

This system is identical to (37) in [25] or (3.10) in [26].

4.2.9 System (4.14)

Remark. If we consider separately the two cases a=0a=0 and a≠0a\neq 0, we can reduce the number of parameters in system (4.14) by scaling variables. In the former case the parameter bb can also be fixed at any nonzero value, while in the latter case only the parameter aa can be scaled away. However, this case distinction is neither necessary nor essential, as is demonstrated below.

If we define new variables ww and WW by

{w≡ux+a2​⟨U,U⟩,W≡⟨U,U⟩​U,\displaystyle\cases{w\equiv u_{x}+\frac{a}{2}\langle U,U\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W\equiv\sqrt{\langle U,U\rangle}U,\cr}

they satisfy the following system:

{wt=wx​x​x+6​w​wx+(b−a24)​⟨W,W⟩x,Wt=2​(w​W)x.\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=w_{xxx}+6ww_{x}+\bigl(b-\frac{a^{2}}{4}\bigr)\langle W,W\rangle_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W_{t}=2(wW)_{x}.\cr} (4.49)

Thus the essential parameter is b−a2/4b-a^{2}/4 rather than aa or bb. If b−a2/4≠0b-a^{2}/4\neq 0, system (4.49) coincides with the multi-component Zakharov–Ito system (3.5), up to a scaling of variables. When b−a2/4=0b-a^{2}/4=0, (4.49) is a triangular system that consists of the KdV equation and the linear equation for WW with KdV-equation-dependent coefficients. This triangular system was studied from a point of view of symmetries in [65] (see also [22, 66, 67]). As we have noted in section 3.2.3, we can relate with WW the inverse square of a solution of the KdV linear problem.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we set

u=q+r,U=q−r,a=1+2​α,b=2​β.u=q+r,\quad U=q-r,\quad a=1+2\alpha,\quad b=2\beta.

Then we can rewrite (4.14) as a system of two symmetrically coupled pKdV equations,

{qt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+(1+α)​(q−r)​qx​x−α⁡(q−r)​rx​x+(3+α)​qx2+(2−2​α)​qx​rx+(1+α)​rx2+(2+4​α)​(q−r)2​qx+β​(q−r)4,rt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+α⁡(q−r)​qx​x−(1+α)​(q−r)​rx​x+(1+α)​qx2+(2−2​α)​qx​rx+(3+α)​rx2+(2+4​α)​(q−r)2​rx+β​(q−r)4.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+(1+\alpha)(q-r)q_{xx}-\alpha(q-r)r_{xx}+(3+\alpha)q_{x}^{2}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+(2-2\alpha)q_{x}r_{x}+(1+\alpha)r_{x}^{2}+(2+4\alpha)(q-r)^{2}q_{x}+\beta(q-r)^{4}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+\alpha(q-r)q_{xx}-(1+\alpha)(q-r)r_{xx}+(1+\alpha)q_{x}^{2}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+(2-2\alpha)q_{x}r_{x}+(3+\alpha)r_{x}^{2}+(2+4\alpha)(q-r)^{2}r_{x}+\beta(q-r)^{4}.\cr} (4.50)

This system is identical to (12) in [25]. Foursov claimed in [25] that this system was either reduced to the representative case α=0\alpha=0 (a=1)(a=1) or decoupled by a linear change of dependent variables. However, in fact this is not true. As far as we consider a linear change of variables, we need one more representative case, α=−12\alpha=-{1\over 2} (a=0)(a=0), in which (4.50) cannot be decoupled. Therefore, we can say that (at least) one system is missing from the final list of Foursov–Olver given in [26].

4.2.10 System (4.15)

System (4.15) is merely a potential form of the Jordan KdV system (3.4). We see in section 4.2.22 that this system is also connected with system (4.27) through a Miura-type transformation.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=12​(q+r),U=i2​(q−r).u=\frac{1}{2}(q+r),\quad U=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}(q-r).

Then (4.15) is decoupled into two pKdV equations,

{qt=qx​x​x+3​qx2,rt=rx​x​x+3​rx2.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=q_{xxx}+3q_{x}^{2}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=r_{xxx}+3r_{x}^{2}.\cr}

This corresponds to (27) in [25].

4.2.11 System (4.16)

System (4.16) is connected with system (4.28) through a Miura-type transformation. We discuss the integrability of these two systems in section 4.2.23.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=3​(q−r).u=q+r,\quad U=\sqrt{3}(q-r).

Then we can rewrite (4.16) as a system of two symmetrically coupled pKdV equations,

{qt=qx​x​x+3​(q−r)​qx​x+3​(qx+rx)​qx+3​(q−r)2​qx,rt=rx​x​x−3​(q−r)​rx​x+3​(qx+rx)​rx+3​(q−r)2​rx.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=q_{xxx}+3(q-r)q_{xx}+3(q_{x}+r_{x})q_{x}+3(q-r)^{2}q_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=r_{xxx}-3(q-r)r_{xx}+3(q_{x}+r_{x})r_{x}+3(q-r)^{2}r_{x}.\cr}

This system coincides with (34) in [25] or (3.9) in [26].

4.2.12 System (4.17)

System (4.17) is connected with system (4.29) through a Miura-type transformation. We discuss the integrability of these two systems in section 4.2.24.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=12​(q+r),U=62​(q−r).u=\frac{1}{2}(q+r),\quad U=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}(q-r).

Then we can rewrite (4.17) as a system of two symmetrically coupled pKdV equations,

{qt=qx​x​x+3​(q−r)​qx​x+3​qx2+3​(q−r)2​qx,rt=rx​x​x−3​(q−r)​rx​x+3​rx2+3​(q−r)2​rx.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=q_{xxx}+3(q-r)q_{xx}+3q_{x}^{2}+3(q-r)^{2}q_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=r_{xxx}-3(q-r)r_{xx}+3r_{x}^{2}+3(q-r)^{2}r_{x}.\cr}

This system coincides with (28) in [25] or (3.8) in [26].

4.2.13 System (4.18)

System (4.18) is connected with system (4.30) through a Miura-type transformation. We discuss the integrability of these two systems in section 4.2.25.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=3​(q−r).u=q+r,\quad U={\sqrt{3}}(q-r).

Then we can rewrite (4.18) as a system of two symmetrically coupled pKdV equations,

{qt=−12​qx​x​x+32​rx​x​x−6​(q−r)​rx​x+6​rx2+12​(q−r)2​rx+3​(q−r)4,rt=32​qx​x​x−12​rx​x​x+6​(q−r)​qx​x+6​qx2+12​(q−r)2​qx+3​(q−r)4.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{3}{2}r_{xxx}-6(q-r)r_{xx}+6r_{x}^{2}+12(q-r)^{2}r_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+3(q-r)^{4}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\frac{3}{2}q_{xxx}-\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+6(q-r)q_{xx}+6q_{x}^{2}+12(q-r)^{2}q_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+3(q-r)^{4}.\cr}

This system is identical to (13) in [25] with α=6\alpha=6. Thus, it is equivalent to (41) in [25] or (3.12) in [26], up to a linear change of dependent variables.

4.2.14 System (4.19)

For system (4.19), if we introduce a new variable ww by

w≡ux+2​⟨U,U⟩,w\equiv u_{x}+2\langle U,U\rangle, (4.51)

it solves the KdV equation,

wt=wx​x​x+2​w​wx.w_{t}=w_{xxx}+2ww_{x}. (4.52a)
Therefore, system (4.19) is reduced to a triangular form. The equation for UU is rewritten in terms of ww as
Ut=4​Ux​x​x+wx​U+2​w​Ux.U_{t}=4U_{xxx}+w_{x}U+2wU_{x}. (4.52b)

We note that the vector equation (4.52b) is of the same form as the time part of the linear problem for the KdV equation (4.52a). This relation between system (4.19) and the KdV equation resembles the relation between the 5th 5^{\mbox{\scriptsize th }}order symmetry of system (4.11) and the Kaup–Kupershmidt equation shown in section 4.2.6. A recursion operator and a Lax representation for the triangular system (4.52b) were given in [67] and [24], respectively. Once we obtain w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) and U⁡(x,t)U(x,t), we can determine u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) by using (4.51).

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=6​(q+r),U=3​i​(q−r).u=6(q+r),\quad U={\sqrt{3}}\hskip 1.0pt\mathrm{i}(q-r).

Then we can rewrite (4.19) as a system of two symmetrically coupled pKdV equations,

{qt=52​qx​x​x−32​rx​x​x+6​(q−r)​qx​x+6​qx2+12​qx​rx−6​rx2−12​(q−r)2​(qx−rx)−3​(q−r)4,rt=−32​qx​x​x+52​rx​x​x−6​(q−r)​rx​x−6​qx2+12​qx​rx+6​rx2+12​(q−r)2​(qx−rx)−3​(q−r)4.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\frac{5}{2}q_{xxx}-\frac{3}{2}r_{xxx}+6(q-r)q_{xx}+6q_{x}^{2}+12q_{x}r_{x}-6r_{x}^{2}\cr\qquad\mbox{}-12(q-r)^{2}(q_{x}-r_{x})-3(q-r)^{4}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=-\frac{3}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{5}{2}r_{xxx}-6(q-r)r_{xx}-6q_{x}^{2}+12q_{x}r_{x}+6r_{x}^{2}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+12(q-r)^{2}(q_{x}-r_{x})-3(q-r)^{4}.\cr}

This system coincides with (42) in [25] or (3.13) in [26].

4.2.15 System (4.20)

For system (4.20), if we introduce a new variable ww by

w≡−ux+12​u2−12​⟨U,U⟩,w\equiv-u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle, (4.53)

it solves the KdV equation,

wt=wx​x​x−3​w​wx.w_{t}=w_{xxx}-3ww_{x}. (4.54a)
Therefore, system (4.20) is reduced to a triangular form. Still, it is a very interesting system. To see this, we rewrite the equation for uu in terms of ww as
ut=−2​ux2+u2​ux−3​w​ux−wx​u−wx​x.u_{t}=-2u_{x}^{2}+u^{2}u_{x}-3wu_{x}-w_{x}u-w_{xx}. (4.54b)

Then, the reduction w=0w=0 changes this equation to a nontrivial closed equation for uu. With a rescaling of variables, it reads

ut=ux​(ux−u2).u_{t}=u_{x}(u_{x}-u^{2}). (4.55)

Equation (4.55) possesses an infinite set of commuting symmetries

uτn=ux​(ux−u2)n,n∈ℝ.u_{\tau_{n}}=u_{x}(u_{x}-u^{2})^{n},\quad n\in{\mathbb{R}}.

We can easily obtain a travelling-wave solution of (4.55) with two arbitrary constants [68], which is called a complete solution in the theory of partial differential equations. However, we do not know any explicit formula for the general solution of (4.55). Using (4.53), we can rewrite the equation for UU as a linear equation with a u,wu,w-dependent coefficient.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=q−r.u=q+r,\quad U=q-r.

Then we can rewrite (4.20) as a system of two symmetrically coupled mKdV equations,

{qt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+12​(q−r)​(qx​x−rx​x)−(qx−rx)​rx+(q2−5​q​r)​qx−(q2+q​r)​rx,rt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+12​(q−r)​(qx​x−rx​x)+(qx−rx)​qx−(q​r+r2)​qx+(−5​q​r+r2)​rx.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}(q-r)(q_{xx}-r_{xx})-(q_{x}-r_{x})r_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+(q^{2}-5qr)q_{x}-(q^{2}+qr)r_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}(q-r)(q_{xx}-r_{xx})+(q_{x}-r_{x})q_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}-(qr+r^{2})q_{x}+(-5qr+r^{2})r_{x}.\cr}

This system coincides with (57) in [25] or (3.18) in [26], up to a scaling of variables.

4.2.16 System (4.21)

In system (4.21), uu and ⟨U,U⟩\langle U,U\rangle satisfy the same equations as in system (4.20). Thus, if we define ww by (4.53), we obtain (4.54a) and (4.54b) again. The only difference between the two systems (4.21) and (4.20) lies in the forms of equations for UU, which can be rewritten as linear equations with u,wu,w-dependent coefficients.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, (4.21) is identical to (4.20). Thus, through symmetrization, we just obtain the same result as in section 4.2.15.

4.2.17 System (4.22)

System (4.22) has already been obtained in [69] as a reduction of a bi-Hamiltonian system (see also [70]). If we introduce a new variable ww by

w≡−ux+12​u2−12​⟨U,U⟩,w\equiv-u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle,

it solves the KdV equation,

wt=wx​x​x−3​w​wx.w_{t}=w_{xxx}-3ww_{x}. (4.56)

Therefore, system (4.22) is reduced to a triangular form. Substituting 12​⟨U,U⟩=−ux+12​u2−w\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle=-u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}-w into the equations for uu and UU respectively, we obtain

{ut=−(w​u+wx)x,Ut=−(w​U)x.\displaystyle\cases{u_{t}=-(wu+w_{x})_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=-(wU)_{x}.\cr}

Thus the reduction w=0w=0 is trivial in this system. We mention again (cf. section 4.2.9) that the above equation for UU coupled to the KdV equation (4.56) was studied in [65].

Remark. Actually, a one-parameter deformation of system (4.22),

{ut=3​a​ux+ux​x​x−32​u2​ux+12​ux​⟨U,U⟩+u⁡⟨U,Ux⟩+⟨U,Ux​x⟩+⟨Ux,Ux⟩,Ut=a​Ux+ux​x​U+ux​Ux−u​ux​U−12​u2​Ux+12​⟨U,U⟩​Ux+⟨U,Ux⟩​U,\displaystyle\cases{u_{t}=3au_{x}+u_{xxx}-\frac{3}{2}u^{2}u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle+u\langle U,U_{x}\rangle+\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle+\langle U_{x},U_{x}\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=aU_{x}+u_{xx}U+u_{x}U_{x}-uu_{x}U-\frac{1}{2}u^{2}U_{x}+\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle U_{x}+\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U,\cr} (4.57)

is still integrable. Indeed, if we introduce ww in this case by

w≡−a−ux+12​u2−12​⟨U,U⟩,w\equiv-a-u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle,

system (4.57) is changed into the following system:

{wt=wx​x​x−3​w​wx+2​a​⟨U,Ux⟩,Ut=−(w​U)x.\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=w_{xxx}-3ww_{x}+2a\langle U,U_{x}\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=-(wU)_{x}.\cr}

When a≠0a\neq 0, this system coincides with the multi-component Zakharov–Ito system (3.5), up to a scaling of variables.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=q−r.u=q+r,\quad U=q-r.

Then we can rewrite (4.22) as a system of two symmetrically coupled mKdV equations,

{qt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+(q−r)​qx​x+(qx−rx)​qx−4​q​r​qx−2​q2​rx,rt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x−(q−r)​rx​x−(qx−rx)​rx−2​r2​qx−4​q​r​rx.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+(q-r)q_{xx}+(q_{x}-r_{x})q_{x}-4qrq_{x}-2q^{2}r_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}-(q-r)r_{xx}-(q_{x}-r_{x})r_{x}-2r^{2}q_{x}-4qrr_{x}.\cr}

This system coincides with (58) in [25] or (3.19) in [26].

4.2.18 System (4.23)

For system (4.23), if we introduce a new variable ww by

w≡−ux+12​u2−12​⟨U,U⟩,w\equiv-u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle,

it satisfies the KdV equation,

wt=wx​x​x−3​w​wx.w_{t}=w_{xxx}-3ww_{x}. (4.58a)
Therefore, system (4.23) is reduced to a triangular form. The equation for uu is rewritten in terms of ww as
ut=−u2​ux+12​u4−wx​x+w​ux−wx​u−2​w​u2+2​w2.u_{t}=-u^{2}u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u^{4}-w_{xx}+wu_{x}-w_{x}u-2wu^{2}+2w^{2}. (4.58b)

The triangular system (4.58b) possesses (at least) two higher symmetries. The first higher symmetry is given by

{wt5=wx​x​x​x​x−5​w​wx​x​x−10​wx​wx​x+152​w2​wx,ut5=−12​u4​w+2​u2​w2−2​w3+u2​w​ux−12​w2​ux−u3​wx+5​u​w​wx+2​u​ux​wx+3​wx2−u2​wx​x+5​w​wx​x+ux​wx​x−u​wx​x​x−wx​x​x​x,\displaystyle\cases{w_{t_{5}}=w_{xxxxx}-5ww_{xxx}-10w_{x}w_{xx}+\frac{15}{2}w^{2}w_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr u_{t_{5}}=-\frac{1}{2}u^{4}w+2u^{2}w^{2}-2w^{3}+u^{2}wu_{x}-\frac{1}{2}w^{2}u_{x}-u^{3}w_{x}+5uww_{x}\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+2uu_{x}w_{x}+3w_{x}^{2}-u^{2}w_{xx}+5ww_{xx}+u_{x}w_{xx}-uw_{xxx}-w_{xxxx},\cr}

which obviously vanishes under the reduction w=0w=0. Similarly, the second one vanishes under the same reduction. On the other hand, the reduction w=0w=0 changes (4.58b) to a nontrivial closed equation for uu,

ut=−u2​ux+12​u4.u_{t}=-u^{2}u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u^{4}.

As far as we could check with the help of a computer, this equation seems to have no polynomial higher symmetry. We can construct its general solution in implicit form using the method of characteristic curves.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=q−r.u=q+r,\quad U=q-r.

Then we can rewrite (4.23) as a system of two symmetrically coupled mKdV equations,

{qt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+12​(q−r)​(qx​x−rx​x)−(qx−rx)​rx−(3​q​r+r2)​qx+(−3​q​r+r2)​rx+12​(q−r)3​q,rt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+12​(q−r)​(qx​x−rx​x)+(qx−rx)​qx+(q2−3​q​r)​qx−(q2+3​q​r)​rx−12​(q−r)3​r.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}(q-r)(q_{xx}-r_{xx})-(q_{x}-r_{x})r_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}-(3qr+r^{2})q_{x}+(-3qr+r^{2})r_{x}+\frac{1}{2}(q-r)^{3}q\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}(q-r)(q_{xx}-r_{xx})+(q_{x}-r_{x})q_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+(q^{2}-3qr)q_{x}-(q^{2}+3qr)r_{x}-\frac{1}{2}(q-r)^{3}r.\cr}

This system coincides with (61) in [25] or (3.20) in [26], up to a scaling of variables.

4.2.19 System (4.24)

For system (4.24), if we introduce a new variable ww by

w≡−ux+12​u2−12​⟨U,U⟩,w\equiv-u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}-\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle, (4.59)

it satisfies the KdV equation,

wt=wx​x​x−3​w​wx.w_{t}=w_{xxx}-3ww_{x}.

Therefore, system (4.24) is rewritten in a triangular form. Substituting 12​⟨U,U⟩=−ux+12​u2−w\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle=-u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}u^{2}-w into the equations for uu and UU respectively, we obtain

{ut=−wx​u−12​w​u2−wx​x+w2,Ut=−12​(wx+w​u)​U.\displaystyle\cases{u_{t}=-w_{x}u-\frac{1}{2}wu^{2}-w_{xx}+w^{2}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=-\frac{1}{2}(w_{x}+wu)U.\cr} (4.60)

Thus the reduction w=0w=0 is trivial in this system. We note that in (4.60) no term involves xx-derivatives of u,Uu,\hskip 1.0ptU such as ux,Ux,ux​x,Ux​xu_{x},\hskip 1.0ptU_{x},\hskip 1.0ptu_{xx},\hskip 1.0ptU_{xx}. Then, for a given solution of the KdV equation w⁡(x,t)w(x,t), the equation for u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) can be regarded as a Riccati equation with xx fixed. Once we obtain w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) and u⁡(x,t)u(x,t), we can integrate the equation for UU as

U(x,t)=e−12∫t0(wx+wu)dt′U(x,0).U(x,t)={\rm e}^{-\frac{1}{2}\int^{t}_{0}(w_{x}+wu){\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptt^{\prime}}U(x,0).

Remark. Actually, system (4.24) is the 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry of a nontrivial 1st 1^{\mbox{\scriptsize st }}order system,

{ut1=ux+12​⟨U,U⟩,Ut1=12​u​U.\displaystyle\cases{u_{t_{1}}=u_{x}+\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t_{1}}=\frac{1}{2}uU.\cr} (4.61)

For this system, ww defined by (4.59) obeys the linear equation wt1=wxw_{t_{1}}=w_{x} and the equation for uu is rewritten as ut1=12​u2−wu_{t_{1}}=\frac{1}{2}u^{2}-w. System (4.61) in the N=1N=1 case as well as its higher symmetries was studied in [56, 71, 72] (see also [73] for its soliton-like solutions).

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=q−r.u=q+r,\quad U=q-r.

Then we can rewrite (4.24) as a system of two symmetrically coupled mKdV equations,

{qt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+14​(q−r)​(3​qx​x−rx​x)+12​(qx−rx)2+12​(q2−6​q​r−r2)​qx−(q2+2​q​r)​rx−q2​r​(q−r),rt=12​qx​x​x+12​rx​x​x+14​(q−r)​(qx​x−3​rx​x)+12​(qx−rx)2−(2​q​r+r2)​qx−12​(q2+6​q​r−r2)​rx+q​r2​(q−r).\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+\frac{1}{4}(q-r)(3q_{xx}-r_{xx})+\frac{1}{2}(q_{x}-r_{x})^{2}\cr\qquad\mbox{}+\frac{1}{2}(q^{2}-6qr-r^{2})q_{x}-(q^{2}+2qr)r_{x}-q^{2}r(q-r)\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\frac{1}{2}q_{xxx}+\frac{1}{2}r_{xxx}+\frac{1}{4}(q-r)(q_{xx}-3r_{xx})+\frac{1}{2}(q_{x}-r_{x})^{2}\cr\qquad\mbox{}-(2qr+r^{2})q_{x}-\frac{1}{2}(q^{2}+6qr-r^{2})r_{x}+qr^{2}(q-r).\cr}

This system coincides with (23) in [25] with α=1\alpha=1, up to a scaling of dependent variables. Thus, it is equivalent to (62) in [25] or (3.21) in [26], up to a linear change of variables.

4.2.20 System (4.25)

System (4.25) is just a disguised form of a single vector equation. Indeed, if we introduce an (N+1)(N+1)-component vector WW by W≡(u,U)=(u,U1,…,UN)W\equiv(u,U)=(u,U_{1},\ldots,U_{N}), system (4.25) can be rewritten in the form

Wt=Wx​x​x+⟨W,W⟩​Wx.\displaystyle W_{t}=W_{xxx}+\langle W,W\rangle W_{x}.

This is a well-known vector mKdV equation and its integrability has been established in the literature [27, 28, 74, 75].

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=12​(q+r),U=i2​(q−r).u=\frac{1}{2}(q+r),\quad U=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}(q-r).

Then we can rewrite (4.25) as a system of two symmetrically coupled mKdV equations,

{qt=qx​x​x+q​r​qx,rt=rx​x​x+q​r​rx.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=q_{xxx}+qrq_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=r_{xxx}+qrr_{x}.\cr}

This system is known as (the non-reduced form of) the complex mKdV equation [76]. It is identical to (43) in [25] or, (3.14) in [26] with a correction of misprints.

4.2.21 System (4.26)

System (4.26) is also a disguised form of a single vector equation. Indeed, if we introduce an (N+1)(N+1)-component vector WW by W≡(u,U)=(u,U1,…,UN)W\equiv(u,U)=(u,U_{1},\ldots,U_{N}), system (4.26) can be rewritten in the form

Wt=Wx​x​x+⟨W,W⟩​Wx+⟨W,Wx⟩​W.\displaystyle W_{t}=W_{xxx}+\langle W,W\rangle W_{x}+\langle W,W_{x}\rangle W.

This is another well-known vector mKdV equation, for which a Lax representation was given in [77] for the N=1N=1 case and in [78] for the general NN case.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=i⁡(q−r).u=q+r,\quad U=\mathrm{i}(q-r).

Then we can rewrite (4.26) as a system of two symmetrically coupled mKdV equations,

{qt=qx​x​x+6​q​r​qx+2​q2​rx,rt=rx​x​x+2​r2​qx+6​q​r​rx.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=q_{xxx}+6qrq_{x}+2q^{2}r_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=r_{xxx}+2r^{2}q_{x}+6qrr_{x}.\cr} (4.62)

This system coincides with (48) in [25] or (3.15) in [26], up to a scaling of variables.

4.2.22 System (4.27)

System (4.27) is known as a Jordan mKdV system [27]. Let us briefly summarize its integrability. It is well-known that the matrix mKdV equation,

Qt=Qx​x​x−3​(Qx​Q2+Q2​Qx),Q_{t}=Q_{xxx}-3(Q_{x}Q^{2}+Q^{2}Q_{x}), (4.63)

admits a Lax representation [52, 75, 78, 79]. Then, system (4.27) is also integrable, because it is obtained from (4.63) through the following reduction:

Q=u​𝟏+∑j=1NUj​𝐞j,{𝐞i,𝐞j}+=−2​δi​j​𝟏.Q=u{\mathbf{1}}+\sum_{j=1}^{N}U_{j}{\mathbf{e}}_{j},\hskip 14.22636pt\{{\mathbf{e}}_{i},{\mathbf{e}}_{j}\}_{+}=-2\delta_{ij}{\mathbf{1}}.

We mention that (4.27) admits a generalization to a system for two vector unknowns preserving the integrability [29].

Relation to systems (3.4)(\ref{cKdV}) and (4.15)(\ref{sol14}). If we define new variables ww and WW by [27]

{w≡±ux−u2+⟨U,U⟩,W≡Ux∓2​u​U,\displaystyle\cases{w\equiv\pm u_{x}-u^{2}+\langle U,U\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W\equiv U_{x}\mp 2uU,\cr}

they satisfy the following system:

{wt=wx​x​x+3​(w2−⟨W,W⟩)x,Wt=Wx​x​x+6​(w​W)x.\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=w_{xxx}+3\bigl(w^{2}-\langle W,W\rangle\bigr)_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W_{t}=W_{xxx}+6(wW)_{x}.\cr}

This system coincides with the Jordan KdV system (3.4) and, through potentiation of it, we obtain system (4.15).

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=12​(q+r),U=i2​(q−r).u=\frac{1}{2}(q+r),\quad U=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{2}(q-r).

Then (4.27) is decoupled into two mKdV equations,

{qt=qx​x​x−6​q2​qx,rt=rx​x​x−6​r2​rx.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=q_{xxx}-6q^{2}q_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=r_{xxx}-6r^{2}r_{x}.\cr}

This corresponds to (50) in [25].

4.2.23 System (4.28)

We note that through introduction of a new scalar variable ww by

w≡ux−u2,w\equiv u_{x}-u^{2},

system (4.28) is transformed to a system of coupled KdV-mKdV type,

{wt=wx​x​x+6​w​wx+wx​⟨U,U⟩+2​w​⟨U,U⟩x+12​⟨U,U⟩x​x​x,Ut=Ux​x​x+3​(w​U)x+⟨U,U⟩​Ux+32​⟨U,U⟩x​U.\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=w_{xxx}+6ww_{x}+w_{x}\langle U,U\rangle+2w\langle U,U\rangle_{x}+\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle_{xxx}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=U_{xxx}+3(wU)_{x}+\langle U,U\rangle U_{x}+\frac{3}{2}\langle U,U\rangle_{x}U.\cr} (4.64)

Let us demonstrate that system (4.28) admits a Lax representation. We consider a pair of linear equations for a column-vector function 𝝍\psi,

𝝍x=U^​𝝍,𝝍t=V^​𝝍,\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}_{x}=\hat{U}\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$},\hskip 14.22636pt\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}_{t}=\hat{V}\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$},

with the matrices U^\hat{U} and V^\hat{V} of the following form:

U^=(−i​ζ​IlQRi​ζ​Im+P),\hat{U}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-\mathrm{i}{\zeta}I_{l}&Q\\ R&\mathrm{i}{\zeta}I_{m}+P\\ \end{array}\right), (4.65)
V^=(−4​i​ζ3​Il−2​i​ζ​Q​R+Qx​R−Q​Rx+2​Q​P​R4​ζ2​Q+2​i​ζ​(Qx+Q​P)−Qx​x−2​Qx​P−Q​Px+2​Q​R​Q−Q​P24​ζ2​R+2​i​ζ​(−Rx+P​R)−Rx​x+Px​R+2​P​Rx+2​R​Q​R−P2​R4​i​ζ3​Im+2​i​ζ​R​Q−Px​x+Rx​Q−R​Qx+Px​P−P​Px+2​P​R​Q+2​R​Q​P−P3−3​gx​P).\hat{V}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c|c}\begin{array}[]{l}-4\mathrm{i}{\zeta}^{3}I_{l}-2\mathrm{i}{\zeta}QR\\ \mbox{}+Q_{x}R-QR_{x}+2QPR\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{l}4{\zeta}^{2}Q+2\mathrm{i}{\zeta}(Q_{x}+QP)-Q_{xx}\\ \mbox{}-2Q_{x}P-QP_{x}+2QRQ-QP^{2}\end{array}\\ \hline\cr\begin{array}[]{l}4{\zeta}^{2}R+2\mathrm{i}{\zeta}(-R_{x}+PR)\\ \mbox{}-R_{xx}+P_{x}R+2PR_{x}\\ \mbox{}+2RQR-P^{2}R\end{array}&\begin{array}[]{l}4\mathrm{i}{\zeta}^{3}I_{m}+2\mathrm{i}{\zeta}RQ-P_{xx}+R_{x}Q\\ \mbox{}-RQ_{x}+P_{x}P-PP_{x}+2PRQ\\ \mbox{}+2RQP-P^{3}-3g_{x}P\end{array}\end{array}\right).

Here, ζ{\zeta} is the spectral parameter, IlI_{l} and ImI_{m} are the l×ll\times l and m×mm\times m unit matrices respectively, QQ, RR and PP are l×ml\times m, m×lm\times l and m×mm\times m matrices respectively, and gg is a scalar function. The compatibility condition 𝝍x​t=𝝍t​x\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}_{xt}=\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}_{tx} implies the so-called zero-curvature condition,

U^t−V^x+U^​V^−V^​U^=O.\hat{U}_{t}-\hat{V}_{x}+\hat{U}\hat{V}-\hat{V}\hat{U}=O.

Then, substituting (4.65) into this condition, we obtain a system of three matrix equations,

{Qt+Qx​x​x+3​(Qx​P)x−3​Qx​R​Q−3​Q​R​Qx+3​Qx​P2+3​Q​Px​P−3​gx​Q​P=O,Rt+Rx​x​x−3​(P​Rx)x−3​Rx​Q​R−3​R​Q​Rx+3​P2​Rx+3​P​Px​R+3​gx​P​R=O,Pt+Px​x​x+3​(gx​P)x−3​(P​R​Q+R​Q​P)x+3​P​Px​P+3​P2​R​Q−3​R​Q​P2=O.\displaystyle\cases{Q_{t}+Q_{xxx}+3(Q_{x}P)_{x}-3Q_{x}RQ-3QRQ_{x}+3Q_{x}P^{2}\cr\quad\mbox{}+3QP_{x}P-3g_{x}QP=O\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr R_{t}+R_{xxx}-3(PR_{x})_{x}-3R_{x}QR-3RQR_{x}+3P^{2}R_{x}\cr\quad\mbox{}+3PP_{x}R+3g_{x}PR=O\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr P_{t}+P_{xxx}+3(g_{x}P)_{x}-3(PRQ+RQP)_{x}+3PP_{x}P\cr\quad\mbox{}+3P^{2}RQ-3RQP^{2}=O.\cr} (4.66)

We note that this system admits the reduction R=QtR={}^{t}\hskip-0.7113ptQ, Pt=−P{}^{t}\hskip-1.42262ptP=-P, where the superscript t denotes the transposition. In particular, if we choose

{Q=(u,W1,…,WN)≡(u,W),R=(uW1⋮WN)=(uWt),P=(0V1⋯VN−V1⋮−VNO)≡(0V−VtO),\displaystyle\cases{Q=(u,W_{1},\ldots,W_{N})\equiv(u,W)\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr R=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u\\ W_{1}\\ \vdots\\ W_{N}\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}u\\ {}^{t}\hskip-0.42677ptW\\ \end{array}\right)\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr P=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&\begin{array}[]{ccc}V_{1}&\cdots&V_{N}\end{array}\\ \begin{array}[]{c}-V_{1}\\ \vdots\\ -V_{N}\end{array}&\mbox{\LARGE$O$}\end{array}\right)\equiv\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&V\\ -{}^{t}\hskip-0.56905ptV&O\\ \end{array}\right),\cr}

system (4.66) is reduced to the system

{ut+ux​x​x−6​u2​ux−3​ux​(⟨W,W⟩+⟨V,V⟩)−3​u​(⟨W,Wx⟩+⟨V,Vx⟩)+3​gx​⟨W,V⟩−3​⟨Wx,V⟩x=0,Wt+Wx​x​x+3​(ux​V)x−3​u​gx​V−3​u​ux​W−3​u2​Wx−3​⟨W,W⟩​Wx−3​⟨W,Wx⟩​W−3​⟨W,V⟩x​V=𝟎,Vt+Vx​x​x+3​(gx​V)x−3​(u2​V)x−3​(⟨W,V⟩​W)x−3​⟨V,Vx⟩​V−3​u​⟨V,V⟩​W+3​u​⟨W,V⟩​V=𝟎,\displaystyle\cases{u_{t}+u_{xxx}-6u^{2}u_{x}-3u_{x}(\langle W,W\rangle+\langle V,V\rangle)-3u(\langle W,W_{x}\rangle+\langle V,V_{x}\rangle)\cr\quad\mbox{}+3g_{x}\langle W,V\rangle-3\langle W_{x},V\rangle_{x}=0\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W_{t}+W_{xxx}+3(u_{x}V)_{x}-3ug_{x}V-3uu_{x}W-3u^{2}W_{x}-3\langle W,W\rangle W_{x}\cr\quad\mbox{}-3\langle W,W_{x}\rangle W-3\langle W,V\rangle_{x}V={\mathbf{0}}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr V_{t}+V_{xxx}+3(g_{x}V)_{x}-3(u^{2}V)_{x}-3(\langle W,V\rangle W)_{x}-3\langle V,V_{x}\rangle V\cr\quad\mbox{}-3u\langle V,V\rangle W+3u\langle W,V\rangle V={\mathbf{0}},\cr} (4.67)

together with one constraint,

(u​Vt​W−u​Wt​V)x−⟨W,V⟩​(Vt​W−Wt​V)=O.(u\,{}^{t}\hskip-0.56905ptVW-u\,{}^{t}\hskip-0.56905ptWV)_{x}-\langle W,V\rangle({}^{t}\hskip-0.56905ptVW-{}^{t}\hskip-0.56905ptWV)=O.

When WW and VV are scalar, i.e. N=1N=1, this constraint is satisfied automatically and we obtain a three-component mKdV system. There is another case, the case W=VW=V, for which the constraint is satisfied. Then, if we set

g=u,W=V=i3​U,g=u,\hskip 14.22636ptW=V=\frac{\mathrm{i}}{\sqrt{3}}U,

and change the sign of time tt (t→−tt\to-t), system (4.67) collapses to system (4.28).

Relation to system (4.16)(\ref{sol19}). If we introduce a new scalar variable vv by

v≡ux−u2+13​⟨U,U⟩,v\equiv u_{x}-u^{2}+\frac{1}{3}\langle U,U\rangle,

system (4.28) is changed into the following system:

{vt=(vx​x+3​v2+v⁡⟨U,U⟩+⟨U,Ux​x⟩)x,Ut=Ux​x​x+3​vx​U+3​v​Ux+⟨U,Ux⟩​U.\displaystyle\cases{v_{t}=\bigl(v_{xx}+3v^{2}+v\langle U,U\rangle+\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle\bigr)_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=U_{xxx}+3v_{x}U+3vU_{x}+\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U.\cr} (4.68)

Then, it is straightforward to obtain (4.16) (for u^\hat{u} and UU) from (4.68) through potentiation v=u^xv=\hat{u}_{x}. It should be mentioned here that the authors encountered two papers [80, 81] on the integrability of (4.68) in the case of scalar UU, after they had obtained all the presented results independently.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=q+r,U=3​(q−r).u=q+r,\quad U=\sqrt{3}(q-r).

Then we can rewrite (4.28) as a system of two symmetrically coupled mKdV equations,

{qt=[qx​x+3​(q−r)​qx+q3−12​q2​r+3​q​r2]x,rt=[rx​x−3​(q−r)​rx+3​q2​r−12​q​r2+r3]x.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\bigl[q_{xx}+3(q-r)q_{x}+q^{3}-12q^{2}r+3qr^{2}\bigr]_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\bigl[r_{xx}-3(q-r)r_{x}+3q^{2}r-12qr^{2}+r^{3}\bigr]_{x}.\cr}

This system coincides with (55) in [25] or (3.17) in [26]. Moreover, if we introduce new variables q^\hat{q} and r^\hat{r} by

q^≡3iqe∫x(q−r)​d​x′,r^≡3ire−∫x(q−r)dx′,\hat{q}\equiv\sqrt{3}\hskip 1.0pt\mathrm{i}\hskip 1.0ptq{\rm e}^{\int^{x}(q-r){\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptx^{\prime}},\hskip 14.22636pt\hat{r}\equiv\sqrt{3}\hskip 1.0pt\mathrm{i}\hskip 1.0ptr{\rm e}^{-\int^{x}(q-r){\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptx^{\prime}},

they satisfy the system of coupled mKdV equations (4.62).

4.2.24 System (4.29)

Through introduction of a new scalar variable ww by

w≡ux−u2,w\equiv u_{x}-u^{2},

system (4.29) is transformed to a system that looks very similar to (4.64),

{wt=wx​x​x+6​w​wx+wx​⟨U,U⟩+2​w​⟨U,U⟩x+12​⟨U,U⟩x​x​x,Ut=Ux​x​x+6​(w​U)x+⟨U,U⟩​Ux+2​⟨U,U⟩x​U.\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=w_{xxx}+6ww_{x}+w_{x}\langle U,U\rangle+2w\langle U,U\rangle_{x}+\frac{1}{2}\langle U,U\rangle_{xxx}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=U_{xxx}+6(wU)_{x}+\langle U,U\rangle U_{x}+2\langle U,U\rangle_{x}U.\cr} (4.69)

System (4.69) is a multi-component generalization of a flow of the Jaulent–Miodek hierarchy [82]. Let us demonstrate that (4.69) admits a Lax representation. We consider a pair of linear equations for a column-vector function 𝝍\psi,

{𝝍x​x+(Q+ζ​R)​𝝍=ζ2​𝝍,𝝍t=(4​ζ2​I+2​ζ​R+2​Q+32​R2)​𝝍x−[ζ​Rx+Qx+34​(R2)x]​𝝍.\displaystyle\cases{\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}_{xx}+(Q+{\zeta}R)\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}={\zeta}^{2}\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}_{t}=\bigl(4{\zeta}^{2}I+2{\zeta}R+2Q+\frac{3}{2}R^{2}\bigr)\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}_{x}-\bigl[{\zeta}R_{x}+Q_{x}+\frac{3}{4}(R^{2})_{x}\bigr]\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}.\cr} (4.70)

Here, ζ{\zeta} is the spectral parameter, and QQ and RR are square matrices with the same dimension. The compatibility condition 𝝍x​x​t=𝝍t​x​x\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}_{xxt}=\mbox{\boldmath$\psi$}_{txx} for (4.70) implies a system of two matrix equations,

{Qt=Qx​x​x+3​(Q2)x+34​(R2)x​x​x+32​R2​Qx+34​[Q​(R2)x+3​(R2)x​Q],Rt=Rx​x​x+3​(Q​R+R​Q)x+34​[3​(R2)x​R+R​(R2)x+2​R2​Rx],\displaystyle\cases{Q_{t}=Q_{xxx}+3(Q^{2})_{x}+\frac{3}{4}(R^{2})_{xxx}+\frac{3}{2}R^{2}Q_{x}+\frac{3}{4}\bigl[Q(R^{2})_{x}+3(R^{2})_{x}Q\bigr]\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr R_{t}=R_{xxx}+3(QR+RQ)_{x}+\frac{3}{4}\bigl[3(R^{2})_{x}R+R(R^{2})_{x}+2R^{2}R_{x}\bigr],\cr} (4.71)

together with one constraint,

[Q,R2]=O.\bigl[Q,R^{2}\bigr]=O.

If we consider the reduction,

Q=w​𝟏,R=63​i​∑j=1NUj​𝐞j,{𝐞i,𝐞j}+=−2​δi​j​𝟏,Q=w{\mathbf{1}},\hskip 14.22636ptR=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{3}\mathrm{i}\sum_{j=1}^{N}U_{j}{\mathbf{e}}_{j},\hskip 14.22636pt\{{\mathbf{e}}_{i},{\mathbf{e}}_{j}\}_{+}=-2\delta_{ij}{\mathbf{1}},

the constraint is automatically satisfied and system (4.71) collapses to system (4.69). This Lax representation for (4.69) can be rewritten as that for (4.29) [83].

Relation to system (4.17)(\ref{sol18}). If we introduce a new scalar variable vv by

v≡ux−u2+16​⟨U,U⟩,v\equiv u_{x}-u^{2}+\frac{1}{6}\langle U,U\rangle, (4.72)

system (4.29) is changed into the following system:

{vt=(vx​x+3​v2+2​v​⟨U,U⟩+⟨U,Ux​x⟩+12​⟨Ux,Ux⟩)x,Ut=Ux​x​x+6​vx​U+6​v​Ux+2​⟨U,Ux⟩​U.\displaystyle\cases{v_{t}=\bigl(v_{xx}+3v^{2}+2v\langle U,U\rangle+\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle+\frac{1}{2}\langle U_{x},U_{x}\rangle\bigr)_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=U_{xxx}+6v_{x}U+6vU_{x}+2\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U.\cr} (4.73)

Then, it is straightforward to obtain (4.17) (for u^\hat{u} and UU) from (4.73) through potentiation v=u^xv=\hat{u}_{x}.

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=12​(q+r),U=62​(q−r).u=\frac{1}{2}(q+r),\quad U=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}(q-r).

Then we can rewrite (4.29) as a system of two symmetrically coupled mKdV equations,

{qt=[qx​x+3​(q−r)​qx+q3−6​q2​r+3​q​r2]x,rt=[rx​x−3​(q−r)​rx+3​q2​r−6​q​r2+r3]x.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\bigl[q_{xx}+3(q-r)q_{x}+q^{3}-6q^{2}r+3qr^{2}\bigr]_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\bigl[r_{xx}-3(q-r)r_{x}+3q^{2}r-6qr^{2}+r^{3}\bigr]_{x}.\cr}

This system coincides with (51) in [25] or (3.16) in [26]. It is known as a flow of the modified Jaulent–Miodek hierarchy [83] (see also (7.37) in [84]). While elaborating on this paper, the authors encountered one paper [85] on the three-component generalization of this flow [(4.29) with N=2N=2].

4.2.25 System (4.30)

For system (4.30), if we define new variables ww and WW by

{w≡ux+u2+16​⟨U,U⟩,W≡Ux+2​u​U,\displaystyle\cases{w\equiv u_{x}+u^{2}+\frac{1}{6}\langle U,U\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W\equiv U_{x}+2uU,\cr} (4.74)

they satisfy the following system:

{wt=wx​x​x−6​w​wx+2​⟨W,Wx⟩,Wt=−2​Wx​x​x+6​w​Wx.\displaystyle\cases{w_{t}=w_{xxx}-6ww_{x}+2\langle W,W_{x}\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr W_{t}=-2W_{xxx}+6wW_{x}.\cr} (4.75)

This system coincides with the multi-component Hirota–Satsuma system (3.6), up to a scaling of variables. The Miura map (4.74) is a multi-component generalization of that for the case of scalar UU in [43, 44] and that for the case of two-component vector UU in [61].

Relation to system (4.18)(\ref{sol20}). If we introduce a new scalar variable vv by

v≡ux−u2−16​⟨U,U⟩,v\equiv u_{x}-u^{2}-\frac{1}{6}\langle U,U\rangle, (4.76)

system (4.30) is changed into the following system (cf. (4.3) in [86]):

{vt=(vx​x+3​v2+4​v​⟨U,U⟩+2​⟨U,Ux​x⟩+⟨Ux,Ux⟩+23​⟨U,U⟩2)x,Ut=−2​Ux​x​x−6​vx​U−6​v​Ux−4​⟨U,Ux⟩​U.\displaystyle\cases{v_{t}=\bigl(v_{xx}+3v^{2}+4v\langle U,U\rangle+2\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle+\langle U_{x},U_{x}\rangle+\frac{2}{3}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}\bigr)_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=-2U_{xxx}-6v_{x}U-6vU_{x}-4\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U.\cr} (4.77)

Then, it is straightforward to obtain (4.18) (for u^\hat{u} and UU) from (4.77) through potentiation v=u^xv=\hat{u}_{x}. Combining (4.76) and (4.74), we obtain the relation v+w=2​uxv+w=2u_{x}, and consequently,

u^+∫xw​d​x′=2​u.\hat{u}+\int^{x}w\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptx^{\prime}=2u.

Using this relation, we can also rewrite (4.74) as a transformation between system (4.18) and the multi-component Hirota–Satsuma system (4.75).

Symmetrization. In the case where UU is scalar, we consider the linear change of variables

u=−12​(q+r),U=62​i​(q−r).u=-\frac{1}{2}(q+r),\quad U=\frac{\sqrt{6}}{2}\mathrm{i}(q-r).

Then we can rewrite (4.30) as a system of two symmetrically coupled mKdV equations,

{qt=[−12​qx​x+32​rx​x+3​(q−r)​qx−2​r3]x,rt=[32​qx​x−12​rx​x−3​(q−r)​rx−2​q3]x.\displaystyle\cases{q_{t}=\bigl[-\frac{1}{2}q_{xx}+\frac{3}{2}r_{xx}+3(q-r)q_{x}-2r^{3}\bigr]_{x}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr r_{t}=\bigl[\frac{3}{2}q_{xx}-\frac{1}{2}r_{xx}-3(q-r)r_{x}-2q^{3}\bigr]_{x}.\cr}

This system is identical to (63) in [25] or (3.22) in [26]. It was found in connection with the Kac–Moody Lie algebras and written in a Hamiltonian form about twenty years ago (cf. the C2(1){\rm C}_{2}^{(1)} case in [43] or the B2(1){\rm B}_{2}^{(1)} case in [44]).

5 The case λ1=λ2=12{\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}={1\over 2}}   -- coupled Ibragimov--Shabat equations --

In this section, we classify 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order and 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order systems in the λ1=λ2=12\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}={1\over 2} (Ibragimov–Shabat weighting [36]) case. In the first part (section 5.1), we present a complete list of such systems with a specific order symmetry. In the second part (section 5.2), we prove that the listed systems are linearizable.

5.1 List of systems with a higher symmetry

The general ansatz for a λ1=λ2=12\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=\frac{1}{2} homogeneous evolutionary system of 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order for a scalar function uu and a vector function UU takes the form

{ut2=a1​ux​x+a2​u2​ux+a3​u5+a4​ux​⟨U,U⟩+a5​u​⟨U,Ux⟩+a6​u3​⟨U,U⟩+a7​u​⟨U,U⟩2,Ut2=a8​Ux​x+a9​u​ux​U+a10​u2​Ux+a11​u4​U+a12​⟨U,U⟩​Ux+a13​⟨U,Ux⟩​U+a14​u2​⟨U,U⟩​U+a15​⟨U,U⟩2​U.\displaystyle\cases{u_{t_{2}}=a_{1}u_{xx}+a_{2}u^{2}u_{x}+a_{3}u^{5}+a_{4}u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle+a_{5}u\langle U,U_{x}\rangle\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+a_{6}u^{3}\langle U,U\rangle+a_{7}u\langle U,U\rangle^{2}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t_{2}}=a_{8}U_{xx}+a_{9}uu_{x}U+a_{10}u^{2}U_{x}+a_{11}u^{4}U+a_{12}\langle U,U\rangle U_{x}\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+a_{13}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U+a_{14}u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle U+a_{15}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U.\cr} (5.1)

The following constraints guarantee the order to be 2 and the system not to be triangular:

(a1,a8)≠(0,0),(a4,a5,a6,a7)≠(0,0,0,0),(a9,a10,a11,a14)≠(0,0,0,0).(a_{1},a_{8})\neq(0,0),\hskip 14.22636pt(a_{4},a_{5},a_{6},a_{7})\neq(0,0,0,0),\hskip 14.22636pt(a_{9},a_{10},a_{11},a_{14})\neq(0,0,0,0).

Similarly, the general ansatz for a 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order system takes the form

{ut3=b1​ux​x​x+b2​u2​ux​x+b3​u​ux2+b4​u4​ux+b5​u7+b6​ux​x​⟨U,U⟩+b7​ux​⟨U,Ux⟩+b8​u​⟨Ux,Ux⟩+b9​u​⟨U,Ux​x⟩+b10​u2​ux​⟨U,U⟩+b11​u3​⟨U,Ux⟩+b12​u5​⟨U,U⟩+b13​ux​⟨U,U⟩2+b14​u​⟨U,U⟩​⟨U,Ux⟩+b15​u3​⟨U,U⟩2+b16​u​⟨U,U⟩3,Ut3=b17​Ux​x​x+b18​u​ux​x​U+b19​ux2​U+b20​u​ux​Ux+b21​u2​Ux​x+b22​u3​ux​U+b23​u4​Ux+b24​u6​U+b25​⟨U,U⟩​Ux​x+b26​⟨U,Ux⟩​Ux+b27​⟨Ux,Ux⟩​U+b28​⟨U,Ux​x⟩​U+b29​u​ux​⟨U,U⟩​U+b30​u2​⟨U,U⟩​Ux+b31​u2​⟨U,Ux⟩​U+b32​u4​⟨U,U⟩​U+b33​⟨U,U⟩2​Ux+b34​⟨U,U⟩​⟨U,Ux⟩​U+b35​u2​⟨U,U⟩2​U+b36​⟨U,U⟩3​U,\displaystyle\cases{u_{t_{3}}=b_{1}u_{xxx}+b_{2}u^{2}u_{xx}+b_{3}uu_{x}^{2}+b_{4}u^{4}u_{x}+b_{5}u^{7}+b_{6}u_{xx}\langle U,U\rangle\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{7}u_{x}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle+b_{8}u\langle U_{x},U_{x}\rangle+b_{9}u\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle+b_{10}u^{2}u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{11}u^{3}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle+b_{12}u^{5}\langle U,U\rangle+b_{13}u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{14}u\langle U,U\rangle\langle U,U_{x}\rangle+b_{15}u^{3}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}+b_{16}u\langle U,U\rangle^{3}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t_{3}}=b_{17}U_{xxx}+b_{18}uu_{xx}U+b_{19}u_{x}^{2}U+b_{20}uu_{x}U_{x}+b_{21}u^{2}U_{xx}\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{22}u^{3}u_{x}U+b_{23}u^{4}U_{x}+b_{24}u^{6}U+b_{25}\langle U,U\rangle U_{xx}+b_{26}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U_{x}\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{27}\langle U_{x},U_{x}\rangle U+b_{28}\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle U+b_{29}uu_{x}\langle U,U\rangle U\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{30}u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle U_{x}+b_{31}u^{2}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U+b_{32}u^{4}\langle U,U\rangle U\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{33}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U_{x}+b_{34}\langle U,U\rangle\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U+b_{35}u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{36}\langle U,U\rangle^{3}U,\cr} (5.2)

for which the following constraints guarantee the order to be 3 and the system not to be triangular: (b1,b17)≠(0,0)(b_{1},b_{17})\neq(0,0) and at least one of b6,…,b16b_{6},\ldots,b_{16} and one of b18,…,b24,b29,…,b32,b35b_{18},\ldots,b_{24},b_{29},\ldots,b_{32},b_{35} must not vanish. However, when we consider a 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry for a 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system, we relax these constraints as follows (cf. section 2): (b1,b17)≠(0,0)(b_{1},b_{17})\neq(0,0) and at least one of b1,…,b16b_{1},\ldots,b_{16} and one of b17,…,b36b_{17},\ldots,b_{36} must not vanish.

Proposition 5.1.

No 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system of the form (5.1)(\ref{l12o2}) with a 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry of the form (5.2)(\ref{l12o3}) or a 4th 4^{\mbox{\scriptsize th }}order symmetry exists.

In addition, system (5.3) admits the reduction u=0u=0 which changes it to a vector analogue of the Ibragimov–Shabat equation [15, 34],

Ut=Ux​x​x+3​⟨U,U⟩​Ux​x+6​⟨U,Ux⟩​Ux+3​⟨Ux,Ux⟩​U+3​⟨U,U⟩2​Ux.U_{t}=U_{xxx}+3\langle U,U\rangle U_{xx}+6\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U_{x}+3\langle U_{x},U_{x}\rangle U+3\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U_{x}. (5.5)

We can linearize (5.3) and (5.4) through the same change of dependent variables. In fact, both of them are 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetries of a nontrivial 1st 1^{\mbox{\scriptsize st }}order system,

{ut1=ux+u⁡⟨U,U⟩,Ut1=−u2​U,\displaystyle\cases{u_{t_{1}}=u_{x}+u\langle U,U\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t_{1}}=-u^{2}U,\cr} (5.6)

which is naturally linearizable in the same way.
