6 The case λ1=13{\lambda_{1}=\frac{1}{3}}, λ2=23{\lambda_{2}=\frac{2}{3}}   -- negative results --

In this section, we search for 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order and 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order systems with a specific order symmetry in the case of λ1=13\lambda_{1}=\frac{1}{3}, λ2=23\lambda_{2}=\frac{2}{3}. However, the results turn out to be negative, as is shown below.

The general ansatz for a λ1=13\lambda_{1}=\frac{1}{3}, λ2=23\lambda_{2}=\frac{2}{3} homogeneous evolutionary system of 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order for a scalar function uu and a vector function UU takes the form

{ut2=a1​ux​x+a2​u3​ux+a3​u7+a4​⟨U,Ux⟩+a5​u3​⟨U,U⟩,Ut2=a6​Ux​x+a7​u2​ux​U+a8​u3​Ux+a9​u6​U+a10​u2​⟨U,U⟩​U.\displaystyle\cases{u_{t_{2}}=a_{1}u_{xx}+a_{2}u^{3}u_{x}+a_{3}u^{7}+a_{4}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle+a_{5}u^{3}\langle U,U\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t_{2}}=a_{6}U_{xx}+a_{7}u^{2}u_{x}U+a_{8}u^{3}U_{x}+a_{9}u^{6}U+a_{10}u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle U.\cr} (6.1)

The following constraints guarantee the order to be 2 and the system not to be triangular:

(a1,a6)≠(0,0),(a4,a5)≠(0,0),(a7,a8,a9,a10)≠(0,0,0,0).(a_{1},a_{6})\neq(0,0),\hskip 14.22636pt(a_{4},a_{5})\neq(0,0),\hskip 14.22636pt(a_{7},a_{8},a_{9},a_{10})\neq(0,0,0,0).

Similarly, the general ansatz for a 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order system takes the form

{ut3=b1​ux​x​x+b2​u3​ux​x+b3​u2​ux2+b4​u6​ux+b5​u10+b6​⟨U,Ux​x⟩+b7​⟨Ux,Ux⟩+b8​u2​ux​⟨U,U⟩+b9​u3​⟨U,Ux⟩+b10​u6​⟨U,U⟩+b11​u2​⟨U,U⟩2,Ut3=b12​Ux​x​x+b13​u2​ux​x​U+b14​u​ux2​U+b15​u2​ux​Ux+b16​u3​Ux​x+b17​u5​ux​U+b18​u6​Ux+b19​u9​U+b20​u​ux​⟨U,U⟩​U+b21​u2​⟨U,U⟩​Ux+b22​u2​⟨U,Ux⟩​U+b23​u5​⟨U,U⟩​U+b24​u​⟨U,U⟩2​U,\displaystyle\cases{u_{t_{3}}=b_{1}u_{xxx}+b_{2}u^{3}u_{xx}+b_{3}u^{2}u_{x}^{2}+b_{4}u^{6}u_{x}+b_{5}u^{10}+b_{6}\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{7}\langle U_{x},U_{x}\rangle+b_{8}u^{2}u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle+b_{9}u^{3}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle+b_{10}u^{6}\langle U,U\rangle\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{11}u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t_{3}}=b_{12}U_{xxx}+b_{13}u^{2}u_{xx}U+b_{14}uu_{x}^{2}U+b_{15}u^{2}u_{x}U_{x}+b_{16}u^{3}U_{xx}\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{17}u^{5}u_{x}U+b_{18}u^{6}U_{x}+b_{19}u^{9}U+b_{20}uu_{x}\langle U,U\rangle U\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{21}u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle U_{x}+b_{22}u^{2}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U+b_{23}u^{5}\langle U,U\rangle U\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{24}u\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U,\cr} (6.2)

for which the following constraints guarantee the order to be 3 and the system not to be triangular: (b1,b12)≠(0,0)(b_{1},b_{12})\neq(0,0) and at least one of b6,…,b11b_{6},\ldots,b_{11} and one of b13,…,b24b_{13},\ldots,b_{24} must not vanish. However, when we consider a 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry for a 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system, we relax these constraints as follows (cf. section 2): (b1,b12)≠(0,0)(b_{1},b_{12})\neq(0,0) and at least one of b1,…,b11b_{1},\ldots,b_{11} and one of b12,…,b24b_{12},\ldots,b_{24} must not vanish.

Proposition 6.1.

No 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system of the form (6.1)(\ref{l1323o2}) with a 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry of the form (6.2)(\ref{l1323o3}) or a 4th 4^{\mbox{\scriptsize th }}order symmetry exists.

Proposition 6.2.

No 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order system of the form (6.2)(\ref{l1323o3}) with a 5th 5^{\mbox{\scriptsize th }}order symmetry exists.

7 The case λ1=23{\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{3}}, λ2=13{\lambda_{2}=\frac{1}{3}}

In this section, we classify 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order and 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order systems in the case of λ1=23\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{3}, λ2=13\lambda_{2}=\frac{1}{3}. In the first part (section 7.1), we present complete lists of such systems with a specific order symmetry. In the second part (section 7.2), we prove that the listed systems are linearizable.

7.1 Lists of systems with a higher symmetry

The general ansatz for a λ1=23\lambda_{1}=\frac{2}{3}, λ2=13\lambda_{2}=\frac{1}{3} homogeneous evolutionary system of 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order for a scalar function uu and a vector function UU takes the form

{ut2=a1​ux​x+a2​u4+a3​⟨U,Ux​x⟩+a4​⟨Ux,Ux⟩+a5​u3​⟨U,U⟩+a6​u2​⟨U,U⟩2+a7​u​⟨U,U⟩3+a8​⟨U,U⟩4,Ut2=a9​Ux​x+a10​u3​U+a11​u2​⟨U,U⟩​U+a12​u​⟨U,U⟩2​U+a13​⟨U,U⟩3​U.\displaystyle\cases{u_{t_{2}}=a_{1}u_{xx}+a_{2}u^{4}+a_{3}\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle+a_{4}\langle U_{x},U_{x}\rangle+a_{5}u^{3}\langle U,U\rangle\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+a_{6}u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}+a_{7}u\langle U,U\rangle^{3}+a_{8}\langle U,U\rangle^{4}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t_{2}}=a_{9}U_{xx}+a_{10}u^{3}U+a_{11}u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle U+a_{12}u\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U+a_{13}\langle U,U\rangle^{3}U.\cr} (7.1)

The following constraints guarantee the order to be 2 and the system not to be triangular:

(a1,a3,a9)≠(0,0,0),(a3,a4,a5,a6,a7,a8)≠(0,0,0,0,0,0),\displaystyle(a_{1},a_{3},a_{9})\neq(0,0,0),\hskip 14.22636pt(a_{3},a_{4},a_{5},a_{6},a_{7},a_{8})\neq(0,0,0,0,0,0),
(a10,a11,a12)≠(0,0,0).\displaystyle(a_{10},a_{11},a_{12})\neq(0,0,0).

Similarly, the general ansatz for a 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order system takes the form

{ut3=b1​ux​x​x+b2​u3​ux+b3​⟨U,Ux​x​x⟩+b4​⟨Ux,Ux​x⟩+b5​u2​ux​⟨U,U⟩+b6​u3​⟨U,Ux⟩+b7​u​ux​⟨U,U⟩2+b8​u2​⟨U,U⟩​⟨U,Ux⟩+b9​ux​⟨U,U⟩3+b10​u​⟨U,U⟩2​⟨U,Ux⟩+b11​⟨U,U⟩3​⟨U,Ux⟩,Ut3=b12​Ux​x​x+b13​u2​ux​U+b14​u3​Ux+b15​u​ux​⟨U,U⟩​U+b16​u2​⟨U,U⟩​Ux+b17​u2​⟨U,Ux⟩​U+b18​ux​⟨U,U⟩2​U+b19​u​⟨U,U⟩2​Ux+b20​u​⟨U,U⟩​⟨U,Ux⟩​U+b21​⟨U,U⟩3​Ux+b22​⟨U,U⟩2​⟨U,Ux⟩​U,\displaystyle\cases{u_{t_{3}}=b_{1}u_{xxx}+b_{2}u^{3}u_{x}+b_{3}\langle U,U_{xxx}\rangle+b_{4}\langle U_{x},U_{xx}\rangle+b_{5}u^{2}u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{6}u^{3}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle+b_{7}uu_{x}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}+b_{8}u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle\langle U,U_{x}\rangle\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{9}u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle^{3}+b_{10}u\langle U,U\rangle^{2}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle+b_{11}\langle U,U\rangle^{3}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t_{3}}=b_{12}U_{xxx}+b_{13}u^{2}u_{x}U+b_{14}u^{3}U_{x}+b_{15}uu_{x}\langle U,U\rangle U\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{16}u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle U_{x}+b_{17}u^{2}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U+b_{18}u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{19}u\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U_{x}+b_{20}u\langle U,U\rangle\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U+b_{21}\langle U,U\rangle^{3}U_{x}\cr\qquad\;\mbox{}+b_{22}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U,\cr} (7.2)

for which the following constraints guarantee the order to be 3 and the system not to be triangular: (b1,b3,b12)≠(0,0,0)(b_{1},b_{3},b_{12})\neq(0,0,0) and at least one of b3,…,b11b_{3},\ldots,b_{11} and one of b13,…,b20b_{13},\ldots,b_{20} must not vanish. However, when we consider a 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry for a 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system, we relax these constraints as follows (cf. section 2): (b1,b3,b12)≠(0,0,0)(b_{1},b_{3},b_{12})\neq(0,0,0) and at least one of b1,…,b11b_{1},\ldots,b_{11} and one of b12,…,b22b_{12},\ldots,b_{22} must not vanish.

Theorem 7.1.

Any 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system of the form (7.1)(\ref{l2313o2}) with a 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry of the form (7.2)(\ref{l2313o3}) has to coincide with the following system up to a scaling of t2,x,u,U⁡(𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸t_{2},x,u,U\,(we omit the subscript of 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁t2)t_{2}):

{ut=ux​x+2​⟨U,Ux​x⟩+2​⟨Ux,Ux⟩+2​u​⟨U,U⟩3+2​⟨U,U⟩4,Ut=−u​⟨U,U⟩2​U−⟨U,U⟩3​U.\displaystyle\cases{u_{t}=u_{xx}+2\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle+2\langle U_{x},U_{x}\rangle+2u\langle U,U\rangle^{3}+2\langle U,U\rangle^{4}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=-u\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U-\langle U,U\rangle^{3}U.\cr} (7.3)
Theorem 7.2.

Any 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system of the form (7.1)(\ref{l2313o2}) with a 4th 4^{\mbox{\scriptsize th }}order symmetry has to coincide with either (7.3)(\ref{l2313-1}) or the following system up to a scaling of t2,x,u,Ut_{2},x,u,U:

{ut=−2​⟨U,Ux​x⟩−2​u3​⟨U,U⟩−6​u2​⟨U,U⟩2−6​u​⟨U,U⟩3−2​⟨U,U⟩4,Ut=Ux​x+u3​U+3​u2​⟨U,U⟩​U+3​u​⟨U,U⟩2​U+⟨U,U⟩3​U.\displaystyle\cases{u_{t}=-2\langle U,U_{xx}\rangle-2u^{3}\langle U,U\rangle-6u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}-6u\langle U,U\rangle^{3}-2\langle U,U\rangle^{4}\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=U_{xx}+u^{3}U+3u^{2}\langle U,U\rangle U+3u\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U+\langle U,U\rangle^{3}U.\cr} (7.4)
Theorem 7.3.

Any 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order system of the form (7.2)(\ref{l2313o3}) with a 5th 5^{\mbox{\scriptsize th }}order symmetry has to coincide with either of the following two systems up to a scaling of t3,x,u,U⁡(𝐶𝐿𝑂𝑆𝐸t_{3},x,u,U\,(we omit the subscript of 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁t3)t_{3}):

{ut=ux​x​x+2​⟨U,Ux​x​x⟩+6​⟨Ux,Ux​x⟩+2​ux​⟨U,U⟩3+4​⟨U,U⟩3​⟨U,Ux⟩,Ut=−ux​⟨U,U⟩2​U−2​⟨U,U⟩2​⟨U,Ux⟩​U,\displaystyle\cases{u_{t}=u_{xxx}+2\langle U,U_{xxx}\rangle+6\langle U_{x},U_{xx}\rangle+2u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle^{3}+4\langle U,U\rangle^{3}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=-u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U-2\langle U,U\rangle^{2}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U,\cr} (7.5)
{ut=ux​x​x+2​⟨U,Ux​x​x⟩+6​⟨Ux,Ux​x⟩+2​ux​⟨U,U⟩3+4​⟨U,U⟩3​⟨U,Ux⟩,Ut=−ux​⟨U,U⟩2​U−4​u​⟨U,U⟩​⟨U,Ux⟩​U+4​u​⟨U,U⟩2​Ux−6​⟨U,U⟩2​⟨U,Ux⟩​U+4​⟨U,U⟩3​Ux.\displaystyle\cases{u_{t}=u_{xxx}+2\langle U,U_{xxx}\rangle+6\langle U_{x},U_{xx}\rangle+2u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle^{3}+4\langle U,U\rangle^{3}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle\vskip 4.2679pt,\cr U_{t}=-u_{x}\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U-4u\langle U,U\rangle\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U+4u\langle U,U\rangle^{2}U_{x}\cr\qquad\mbox{}-6\langle U,U\rangle^{2}\langle U,U_{x}\rangle U+4\langle U,U\rangle^{3}U_{x}.\cr} (7.6)

We note that (7.5) is the 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry of the 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order system (7.3).

7.2 Integrability of systems (7.3)–(7.6)

7.2.1 Systems (7.3) and (7.5)

We present a procedure for solving system (7.3) only, because its 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order symmetry (7.5) can be solved in the same way. For system (7.3), if we introduce a new variable ww by

w≡u+⟨U,U⟩,w\equiv u+\langle U,U\rangle, (7.7)

it solves the linear equation,

wt=wx​x.w_{t}=w_{xx}.

Once we know w⁡(x,t)w(x,t) by solving this equation, we obtain from the relation (⟨U,U⟩−2)t=4​w\left(\langle U,U\rangle^{-2}\right)_{t}=4w that

1⟨U⁡(x,t),U⁡(x,t)⟩2=4​∫0tw⁡(x,t′)​d​t′+1⟨U⁡(x,0),U⁡(x,0)⟩2.\frac{1}{\langle U(x,t),U(x,t)\rangle^{2}}=4\int_{0}^{t}w(x,t^{\prime}){\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptt^{\prime}+\frac{1}{\langle U(x,0),U(x,0)\rangle^{2}}.

Then we can determine u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) by using (7.7). Finally, noting the relation (⟨U,U⟩−12​U)t=𝟎\bigl(\langle U,U\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}}U\bigr)_{t}=\mbox{\boldmath$0$}, we obtain the following expression for U⁡(x,t)U(x,t):

U⁡(x,t)=1[1+4​⟨U⁡(x,0),U⁡(x,0)⟩2​∫0tw⁡(x,t′)​d​t′]14​U​(x,0).U(x,t)=\frac{1}{\left[1+4\langle U(x,0),U(x,0)\rangle^{2}\int_{0}^{t}w(x,t^{\prime}){\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptt^{\prime}\right]^{\frac{1}{4}}}U(x,0).

7.2.2 System (7.4)

For system (7.4), we have the relation (u+⟨U,U⟩)t=0(u+\langle U,U\rangle)_{t}=0. Thus, we can set

u+⟨U,U⟩≡ϕ⁡(x),u+\langle U,U\rangle\equiv\phi(x),

where the function ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) does not depend on tt. Then the equation for UU is rewritten in terms of ϕ⁡(x)\phi(x) as

Ut=Ux​x+ϕ3​U.U_{t}=U_{xx}+\phi^{3}U. (7.8)

The solutions of (7.8) are given by

U⁡(x,t)=∫d​λ​eλ​t​Ψ​(x,λ),U(x,t)=\int{\rm d}\hskip 0.0pt\lambda\,{\rm e}^{\lambda t}\Psi(x;\lambda),

where Ψ⁡(x,λ)\Psi(x;\lambda) is a solution of the ordinary differential equation

Ψx​x+ϕ3​Ψ=λ​Ψ.\Psi_{xx}+\phi^{3}\Psi=\lambda\Psi.

The following commutation relation indicates that system (7.4) possesses a polynomial higher symmetry of every even order (cf. [7, 10]):

[∂x2+ϕ3,(∂x2+ϕ3)n]=0,n=1,2,….\left[\partial_{x}^{2}+\phi^{3},\,(\partial_{x}^{2}+\phi^{3})^{n}\right]=0,\hskip 14.22636ptn=1,2,\ldots\,\hskip 1.0pt.

7.2.3 System (7.6)

For system (7.6), if we introduce a new variable ww by

w≡u+⟨U,U⟩,w\equiv u+\langle U,U\rangle,

it solves the linear equation,

wt=wx​x​x.w_{t}=w_{xxx}.

Once we know w⁡(x,t)w(x,t), we obtain from the relation (⟨U,U⟩−2)t=4​wx\left(\langle U,U\rangle^{-2}\right)_{t}=4w_{x} that

1⟨U⁡(x,t),U⁡(x,t)⟩2=4​∫0twx​(x,t′)​d​t′+1⟨U⁡(x,0),U⁡(x,0)⟩2.\frac{1}{\langle U(x,t),U(x,t)\rangle^{2}}=4\int_{0}^{t}w_{x}(x,t^{\prime}){\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptt^{\prime}+\frac{1}{\langle U(x,0),U(x,0)\rangle^{2}}. (7.9)

Then the equation for ⟨U,U⟩−12​U\langle U,U\rangle^{-\frac{1}{2}}U can be rewritten as

(1⟨U,U⟩​U)t\displaystyle\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\langle U,U\rangle}}U\right)_{t} =\displaystyle\hskip-5.69054pt=\hskip-5.69054pt 4​(u+⟨U,U⟩)​⟨U,U⟩2​(1⟨U,U⟩​U)x\displaystyle 4(u+\langle U,U\rangle)\langle U,U\rangle^{2}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\langle U,U\rangle}}U\right)_{x}
=\displaystyle\hskip-5.69054pt=\hskip-5.69054pt 4​w​(x,t)4​∫0twx​(x,t′)​d​t′+1⟨U⁡(x,0),U⁡(x,0)⟩2​(1⟨U,U⟩​U)x.\displaystyle\frac{4w(x,t)}{4\int^{t}_{0}w_{x}(x,t^{\prime}){\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptt^{\prime}+\frac{1}{\langle U(x,0),U(x,0)\rangle^{2}}}\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{\langle U,U\rangle}}U\right)_{x}.

The general solution of this equation is given by

1⟨U,U⟩​Uj=fj​(4​∫0tw⁡(x,t′)​d​t′+∫x1⟨U⁡(x′,0),U⁡(x′,0)⟩2​d​x′),\displaystyle\frac{1}{\sqrt{\langle U,U\rangle}}U_{j}=f_{j}\left(4\int^{t}_{0}w(x,t^{\prime}){\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptt^{\prime}+\int^{x}\frac{1}{\langle U(x^{\prime},0),U(x^{\prime},0)\rangle^{2}}\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptx^{\prime}\right),
j=1,2,…,N,\displaystyle\hskip 227.62204ptj=1,2,\ldots,N, (7.10)

where f1​(z),…,fN​(z)f_{1}(z),\ldots,f_{N}(z) are arbitrary functions of zz, except that they must satisfy one constraint, ∑j=1N[fj​(z)]2=1\sum_{j=1}^{N}\left[f_{j}(z)\right]^{2}=1. Combining (7.10) with (7.9), we arrive at the following formula:

Uj(x,t)=1(ξx)14fj(ξ),j=1,2,…,N,U_{j}(x,t)=\frac{1}{(\xi_{x})^{\frac{1}{4}}}f_{j}(\xi),\hskip 14.22636ptj=1,2,\ldots,N,

where ξ⁡(x,t)≡4​∫0tw⁡(x,t′)​d​t′+∫x⟨U⁡(x′,0),U⁡(x′,0)⟩−2​d​x′\xi(x,t)\equiv 4\int^{t}_{0}w(x,t^{\prime}){\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptt^{\prime}+\int^{x}\langle U(x^{\prime},0),U(x^{\prime},0)\rangle^{-2}{\rm d}\hskip 0.0ptx^{\prime}.

8 Concluding remarks

In this paper, we have presented a classification of integrable evolutionary systems in 1+11+1 dimensions for one scalar unknown u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) and one vector unknown U⁡(x,t)U(x,t). We focused on polynomial systems that are homogeneous under a suitable weighting of ∂x\partial_{x}, ∂t\partial_{t}, u⁡(x,t)u(x,t), U⁡(x,t)U(x,t), and considered five distinct weightings for u,Uu,\hskip 1.0ptU relative to a fixed weight of ∂x\partial_{x}. Then, with the help of a computer algebra program, we obtained the complete lists, up to a scaling of variables, of 2nd 2^{\mbox{\scriptsize nd }}order systems with a 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order or a 4th 4^{\mbox{\scriptsize th }}order symmetry and 3rd 3^{\mbox{\scriptsize rd }}order systems with a 5th 5^{\mbox{\scriptsize th }}order symmetry. We demonstrated the integrability of nearly all listed systems by constructing a Lax representation or a linearizing transformation, or, in some cases, by identifying an integrable closed subsystem contained in the system under investigation.

The following tables give a quick overview of the systems found. Note we use “MT” as an abbreviation for “Miura-type transformation”, including Miura map plus potentiation. In these tables, we set the weight of ∂x\partial_{x} at unity, without any loss of generality. For full details regarding Lax representations, transformations, references, etc., the reader is referred to the corresponding part of the paper identified through the equation number. Here, we would like to make a few remarks on our classification results:

  • •

    The most interesting classification results are obtained for the case λ1=λ2=1\lambda_{1}=\lambda_{2}=1, namely, the Burgers/pKdV/mKdV weighting. The lists in this case consist of a large number of systems, which are shown to have a very wide variety of underlying structures. We compared these lists thoroughly with the lists of two-component systems by Foursov–Olver [18, 25, 26], refined and generalized their work, as described in the introduction.

  • •

    We found a number of pairs/triplets of scalar-vector systems connected through transformations of dependent variables. Besides standard Miura transformations that map both the scalar and vector variables to new ones (see, e.g. (4.44)), we also found Miura-type transformations that act only on the scalar variable and do not change the vector variable (see, e.g. (4.46) combined with potentiation v=u^xv=\hat{u}_{x}). For some other systems, we showed that a new scalar variable defined in terms of the old scalar and vector variables satisfies a closed integrable equation, such as the KdV equation or a linear equation.

  • •

    The search for such transformations in our case of scalar-vector systems is simple in comparison to scalar-scalar systems. For instance, the ansatz that a new scalar variable depends on the original vector variable UU only through scalar products ⟨∂xmU,∂xnU⟩\langle\partial_{x}^{m}U,\partial_{x}^{n}U\rangle narrows down the candidates for such transformations considerably. This leads us to the counter-intuitive observation that scalar-vector systems are, in a sense, more tractable than scalar-scalar systems. This is probably one reason why, unlike our work, Foursov and Olver proved integrability1818 18 They discussed the existence of a recursion operator or a bi-Hamiltonian structure. for only a small proportion of their two-component systems [18, 25, 26].

Finally, we mention some problems not solved in this paper:

  • •

    How can the integrability of the three systems (4.5), (4.8) and (4.9) be established along the lines of this paper? The main obstacle is that we know neither a linearizing transformation nor a proper Lax representation for the two-component Burgers system (4.35). The dependence of the functional form of travelling-wave solutions on the boundary conditions and the velocity implies that (4.35) is a highly nontrivial system and not linearizable by a naive extension of the Hopf–Cole transformation.

  • •

    Some scalar-vector systems are converted to a triangular form, i.e. a closed subsystem plus remaining equations coupled to it. When the remaining equations contain a nonlinear PDE in its own variable (cf. (4.54b) or (4.58b)), it seems to be especially difficult to solve them explicitly for a given solution of the subsystem. Is there any method, like an extension of the inverse scattering method, for dealing with such triangular systems analytically?

  • •

    Can one construct an explicit formula for the general solution of (4.55)? This equation is obtained from system (4.20) or (4.21) by converting it to a triangular form and then considering the special case in which the solution of the subsystem, KdV equation in this case, is identically zero.

Although we concentrated our attention on the five distinct weightings for u,Uu,\hskip 1.0ptU in this paper, we also found integrable systems that are homogeneous under a different weighting of variables. Namely, we obtained systems of coupled KdV-mKdV type, e.g. (4.47), (4.64), (4.69) and (4.77)1919 19 We note that, in addition to a scaling of variables, these systems admit another equivalence transformation u~=u+k​⟨U,U⟩\tilde{u}=u+k\langle U,U\rangle, U~=U\hskip 1.0pt\tilde{U}=U., together with the proof of their integrability. We are planning to complete a classification of integrable systems of this type, i.e. scalar-vector systems with weights λ1=2,λ2=1\lambda_{1}=2,\;\lambda_{2}=1, in a subsequent paper. Preliminary results can be viewed on the web page
        http://lie.math.brocku.ca/twolf/htdocs/sv/over.html .
